subsubtopic: DEMAND THAT GENERAL ELECTION BE CALLED-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sick of a government that feeds inflation instead of "wrestling it to the ground", that increases its spending by 20 per cent but asks Canadians to cut their expectations to 6 per cent, that rewards the bureaucracy with 10 per cent to 12 per cent pay increases just before the budget, but that slaps our Armed Forces in the face with a $100 million reduction. I am sick of a government that has killed Canadians' initiative and their incentive to invest in Canada. I am sick of Liberal members who think it is clever, smart, and cute to change Dominion Day to Canada Day. My constituents tell me they are fed up and ask what we can do. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor):
That (a), the disenchanted Liberal members cross the floor; or (b), the Prime Minister give the country some hope by immediately calling an election.

Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The National Council of Welfare, a federally appointed body, set up to advise the Minister of National Health and Welfare about the problems of poor people, has stated that the budget's "social policy aspects will adversely affect thousands of low-income Canadians." The Council estimates that among those who will be hard hurt by the budget proposals are 100,000 pensioners living at or just above the poverty line. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Crosbie):
That the House of Commons condemns the government and, in particular, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, for their callous disregard of the needs of 100,000 senior citizens at or just above the poverty line, whose real income, meagre though it is, will be reduced as a result of the June 28 budget.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the purpose in creating Petro-Canada was that this company would supply "a window on the oil industry" to Canada. But the window has become frosted as Petro-Canada refuses to supply Members of Parliament any detail of the costs of producing gasoline, both leaded and unleaded, or a justification for the difference in price of these products per litre. Since Petro-Canada is "ours", I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):
That Petro-Canada be directed by this House to supply to this House, and to the public generally, a complete breakdown as to its cost of producing gasoline, both leaded and unleaded, and a proper justification for the difference, sometimes as much as 5 cents a litre at the pump, in the price of these gasoline products.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED STOCKPILING OF BASE METALS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the base metal mining industry in Canada faces a bleak winter. In particular, towns based on such mining activity may be decimated due to mass lay-offs because of temporary mine closures resulting from high inventory and low demand.
I believe the federal government should establish a selective strategic base metals stockpile equivalent to a three-month production supply from mines which are facing shutdown during the coming winter, and that such government-owned stockpile inventory be financed by federal government taxation revenues from either the approval of additional gas exports to the United States, from savings resulting from a cutback in oil imports, or borrowings against the base metals stockpiled inventory. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) and the hon. member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner):
That the government immediately undertake to study and implement a government-owned base metals stockpile to alleviate unemployment in the base metal mining industry this coming winter.

subsubtopic: LAY-OFFS IN CAMBRIDGE, ONT.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister, of the minister responsible for employment and of the Minister of Finance, may I put my question to the Acting Prime Minister. As he probably knows, Cambridge is a community of 75,000 people in the heartland of southwestern Ontario. Until this year it had virtually no real unemployment. This morning the mayor of Cambridge telephoned me and advised me that in the first six months of this year 3,629 residents of Cambridge have been placed on indefinite lay-off; in the last year 1,090 people have become unemployed as a result of plant closures, and there are 1,683 temporary lay-offs.
Will the Acting Prime Minister please advise me what to tell my constituents whose hopes and dreams have been dashed, and whose pride has been stifled as a result of unprecedented rates of unemployment in the heartland of industrial Ontario? What will they do?

subtopic: POSITION OF HOME OWNERS RENEWING MORTGAGES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I take it from the hon. member's question that his reference to $3,000 is the grant provision funded by $300 million in the announcement of the Minister of Finance on budget night. This goes to provide grants to purchasers of new homes or to first-time buyers of existing homes.
1 direct the hon. member's attention to a further provision in the budget, that is, the allocation of an additional $50 million designed to fund the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan, which is addressed specifically to the question raised by the hon. member. That plan provides that, in the face of the renewals which the hon. member has mentioned, those people who have to pay more than 30 per cent of their income toward renewal carrying charges will receive a grant of up to $3,000. There is no interest deferral; it is an outright grant which will be of considerable assistance to the Canadians about whom he has talked.

subtopic: CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION POLICY ON RENT INCREASES
CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION POLICY ON RENT INCREASES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the minister responsible for CMHC. It concerns rental rates on the 20,000-odd units which CMHC is renting out, many of which it acquired by reason of foreclosure. I listened carefully to what the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain had to say and the reply, but I am afraid that the reply was somewhat unintelligible. That might have been because the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain did not ask nicely, so I will ask my question nicely and courteously. Is it the policy to escalate rental rates rapidly to bring them into line with so-called market conditions to enhance saleability, or will the 6 per cent guideline apply? Which is it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION POLICY ON RENT INCREASES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the thrust of the questions from the official opposition regarding the portfolio of CMHC under the mortgage insurance fund, for some reason has been the opposite tack to the questions raised today. Many questions by members of the opposition have been directed to me asking why, for example, CMHC is renting properties at what was referred to by hon. members opposite as lower than market rates. For example, they wanted to know why we were offering buydowns in order to dispose of these properties. Now I take it that the hon. gentlemen on the other side have come to the conclusion that in fact the rents are too high. I wish they would be consistent.
The difficulty is that under that fund, and under the National Housing Act, the corporation is required by law to return
July 15, 1982

those funds which were borrowed at the request of the former government under the leadership of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition. Funds were borrowed to take the corporation through a difficult time with increased foreclosures, and we have that obligation under law.

subtopic: CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION POLICY ON RENT INCREASES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I wonder whether that answer was intelligible to you.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, it seems that the policy of the government with respect to wages and salaries is to freeze them by fiat at 6 per cent, whereas when it comes to rents for CMHC, the policy of government is to get them up as quickly as possible. Is that fair?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I take it that this question had something to do with the first question, so in light of that, and with that interpretation, I refer the hon. member to that section in the speech of the Minister of Finance on budget evening where he made reference to the 6 per cent rule and indicated that that would apply generally but that there were some exceptions which could be made. subsubtopic: INCOME LEVEL APPLICABLE TO WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Veterans Affairs. 1 notified him that 1 would be asking this question. The minister is aware that for some time the maximum annual allowable income for veterans receiving the war veterans allowance has been fixed at S3,100 per year. Recently he admitted that this level was too low and promised that he would take steps to correct the problem. What will the new limit be, and when will the minister be presenting his proposal to Treasury Board for approval?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. Bennett Campbell (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: INCOME LEVEL APPLICABLE TO WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his question. We are currently studying the possibility of raising the casual earnings exemption for recipients of war veterans allowance, presently set at $3,100 for married couples and $2,100 for singles. In addition to that, we are also looking at the question of closing the gap on war veterans allowance benefits to those under 65 as compared with those over 65, as well as the question of raising the level of interest deductions allowable under the war veterans allowance. I can tell the hon. member that I raised these three items when I appeared before the standing committee and indicated that 1 was anxious to proceed with all three. I will certainly be pleased to indicate
Oral Questions
that to the hon. member and to all members of the House at a time when we are prepared to go ahead.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister. Could he tell the House whether the legislation will be introduced this fall, this calendar year, and whether it will apply to the 1982 calendar year, so that those veterans who have worked and earned up to $3,100 can continue to work with the assurance that they will be allowed to earn higher incomes, perhaps even up to $5,000, without affecting their allowances for 1982?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. Bennett Campbell (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I cannot give the hon. member the assurance that it will be proceeded with in the fall, but certainly I am hopeful that I will be in a position to see a number of these issues resolved during the fall session. speechtext: Madam Speaker, oil costs are about to jump 10 per cent on September 1 and natural gas is going up at the same time. The cost will jump another 10 per cent next spring thanks to a federal-provincial agreement. Last year the cost of home heating oil went up $400, and the cost of operating an automobile went from $730 to $945. subtopic: APPLICATION OF CONTROL GUIDELINES TO ENERGY PRICES
speechtext: Nothing.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: APPLICATION OF CONTROL GUIDELINES TO ENERGY PRICES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we have a commitment with three producing provinces. One of those agreements was signed with an NDP government in Saskatchewan which my hon. member will remember. APPLICATION OF SATELLITE TECHNOLOGY TO TELEVISION BROADCASTING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Communications. Would the minister be in a position today to announce a policy which would replace the policies that have so far been followed in terms of the implementation of satellite technology for the delivery of television signals? As he knows, the Cancom Company have now scrambled their signals in large areas of rural Canada, particularly the area in northeastern British Columbia that I represent. That area does not have access to television at all. Has the minister arrived at a decision, has that decision been communicated to the CRTC, and what
answers does he have for this large segment of our society that does not have any access to television?

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
subtopic: APPLICATION OF SATELLITE TECHNOLOGY TO TELEVISION BROADCASTING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as the hon. member realizes, I think that the Cancom experience has been a very successful one in allowing most of the outlying regions of the country to obtain decent television coverage from three or four television stations and a number of radio channels. The licensing process has been ongoing. I believe there are over 300 licensees at the moment. I think that the hon. member is concerned about the type of organization that can be licensed by the CRTC. I would undertake to communicate his concerns to the CRTC to determine whether it would indeed be possible to allow the municipalities to become licence holders. That is a matter which I would discuss with the CRTC at this time.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF SATELLITE TECHNOLOGY TO TELEVISION BROADCASTING
speechtext: I appreciate the minister's answer. He understands the peculiar problems in my area which are similar to those in most rural areas in Canada.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: LACK OF TELEVISION RECEPTION IN RURAL AREAS
LACK OF TELEVISION RECEPTION IN RURAL AREAS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the situation is that the CRTC has given licences to operators who are not concerned about coverage to the rural areas and that there will be a need to offer duplicate licences to other operators who are willing to broadcast a signal to outlying areas. This is crucially important for farm communities where people often do not have any access to television and, in terms of official public policy, are denied the benefits of our new technological breakthroughs.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
subtopic: LACK OF TELEVISION RECEPTION IN RURAL AREAS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member raises a very real problem because there are indeed a number of areas in the country where simply cabling a village does not meet any of the requirements of people who live outside the boundaries of the population agglomeration.
I should point out, however, that there is a second problem involved in the rebroadcast type of equipment, in the sense that there is a limited amount of spectrum that is available, and you probably could not license a new operator to rebroadcast four or five channels. Once again, this is a matter that 1 am most sympathetic to, and one of which both my department and the CRTC are aware. I will pursue the matter with them.

PETRO-CANADA SELLING PRICE OF HEATING OIL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I recently talked to a small fuel-oil supplier in my riding who lost a contract for supplying a local municipality with heating oil. Petro-Canada sold them oil at a cost below
July 15, 1982

that at which this supplier could buy it. I now understand that Petro-Canada is sending every household a brochure advertising cheap home fuel. Is it the intention of the minister to force all small fuel companies out of business by letting Petro-Canada sell heating oil at prices so low that they must be subsidized by their own tax dollars?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PETRO-CANADA SELLING PRICE OF HEATING OIL
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there is no subsidization of Petro-Canada to provide cheap prices. As a matter of fact I receive complaints from some members every once in a while that Petro-Canada is charging more than others. Petro-Canada is in a very competitive business and if, in some cases, Petro-Canada ends up causing the consumers to pay less for their fuel than they would otherwise have to pay, I am afraid that I cannot complain about such a situation. The consumers of Canada will benefit from a very active competition in the oil and gas business. Petro-Canada should continue to do its job in that regard. Its instructions are to be an aggressive competitor in the industry and to make sure that the consumers of this country get the best possible deal.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA SELLING PRICE OF HEATING OIL
speechtext: I would like to remind the minister that I recognize, every time I pull into a gas station, that I pay so much to subsidize his Petro-Canada.

speechtext:
To this point the New Democratic Party has put forward 11 speakers on this bill. I suggest that their views have been made known to the House in detail and I doubt if they have much left to add.
I would like to commend members on all sides of the House for their participation in these proceedings on second reading. I can assure members that the points raised have been and will be examined very carefully. I am sure the views expressed will be useful as we proceed through the committee stage of Bill C-124.
There is no need for me to recite the circumstances which led to the necessity for the measures contained in Bill C-124. Members on all sides of the House have recognized the serious economic circumstances of the day. As well, recognition has come from several quarters of the need for the government to provide leadership and an example for other sectors of the economy.
The need for the government to provide a clear, strong signal to serve as an example to other sectors of the economy was never more evident. Bill C-124 should be viewed in that light, not as an attack on the public service of Canada, as has been suggested by some hon. members. There is already mounting evidence that the measures contained in Bill C-124 will provide the kind of example to which other sectors of the economy will respond-will respond in a fashion tailored to their individual circumstances but nonetheless with the same objectives of reducing inflation and protecting our competitive trade position.
I would like to take this opportunity to address several particular points which have been raised during these proceedings. Many speakers have raised the question of the effect of Bill C-124 on the equal pay for work of equal value provisions of the Canadian Human Rights Act. I remind members that in response to a specific question in that regard, I have indicated that it was not the intention that this bill would interfere with those provisions of the Canadian Human Rights Act. I said at the time and I repeat, that to remove any uncertainty in that regard I would be prepared to introduce an appropriate amendment to the bill.
The suspension of collective bargaining rights and the right to strike has also been referred to on a number of occasions. We must keep in mind that this is a limited, short-term program designed to deal with a particular aspect of a difficult economic situation. Other countries, and I note particularly the United Kingdom and France, have taken what I would regard as even more stringent measures.
I would also note that the bill does not abrogate all employ-er/employee relationships. For example, in the federal public service it is my view that most of the consultation which takes
Time Allocation
place at the national joint council can continue during the term that this bill would have application. As I have said before in the House, it is my hope and the hope of the government that that will be the case. The measures contained in Bill C-124 are designed to ensure the continuance of existing bargaining structures and that at the end of the program the normal process of collective bargaining can and will be resumed.
Much has also been made in this House of the provision of the same percentage wage rate increase for all levels of the public service. Controls programs in the past have had the effect of severely disrupting existing, worthwhile management compensation practices. The program envisaged by Bill C-124 is designed not to do that.
It is also clear that the bill contains special provisions for executive levels of the federal public service. Members will recall that the tenth report of the advisory group on executive compensation in the public service recommended a wage rate increase for these levels of 9.5 per cent effective April 1, 1982. The provisions of Bill C-124 postpone the normal review date until July 1 and apply the 6 per cent increase as of that date. No other group is treated in this manner. It is also important to note that the compensation for executive levels of the federal public service trails that of their comparable counterparts in the private sector.
It has also been noted in this House that compensation for the lower levels of the public service tends to be more comparable with the private sector; thus the provision is in fact designed to be an equitable provision of wage restraint for a limited period of time. I emphasize "limited", Mr. Speaker.
In closing, I would again like to thank members of the House for their contribution to the proceedings thus far and I look forward to moving to the next stage, as I hope they do.
Bill C-124 is a necessary provision in these times, undertaken with great reluctance but nevertheless undertaken with the firm resolve that it provides the leadership and example needed to help set us on the road to lower inflation and protection of our competitive trade position.
I was interested in a Gallup poll released today which suggests that 80 per cent of Canadians would accept a 10 per cent pay cut in order to save their jobs; surely asking public servants to accept a 6 per cent pay raise to help save the country is not asking too much by comparison.

How long have economists had to consider the long-term effects of this bill? What chance have union and labour leaders had to consider its ramifications? The government's intention is to trample on public opinion as expressed through Members of Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, we have had this bill for 11 days. The bill was introduced on June 30, but with typical Liberal government trickery it was not distributed until July 5. The Liberals want to shut off the public debate in that short time. It is indecent haste and it is an arrogant abuse of our rights as Members of Parliament. It is not fair to shove this bill through second reading without giving ample time for the public to consider its ramifications.
This government, Mr. Speaker, is cowering in fear of public opinion. After months of delay and indecision while it pushed through the Constitution and raped the energy industry, it now wants to speed up passage of this particular bill. We believe in the restraint which the bill incorporates. We support the concept of restraint on the salaries of Members of Parliament, but we stand for fairness and equity in discussion. The same government which rushes through this bill also rushed through the 11 per cent increase for political assistants to ministers.
Since the last budget was brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) with the concept of wage restraints, we have pointed out the fallacy of the government's position. On the one hand it restrains; on the other hand it increases. Where are the controls on regulatory agencies? Bell Canada applies for a 25 per cent rate increase the day after the finance minister announces restraint. CMHC, a government-owned agency, could hardly wait to raise rents 20 per cent to 42 per cent. Statistics Canada reports to the public that regulated prices-telephones, heating fuel, gasoline, stamps- went up 18 per cent last year. Where is the legislation to control the prices this government has responsibility for? We have developed that theme in question period and pointed out time and time again that the Liberal government is talking out of both sides of its mouth.
In this case, Mr. Speaker, closure is not justified to shut off public debate. What would have happened if the debate on the November 12 budget had been shut off in 11 days? In that case, the Minister of Finance would not have had the opportunity to make 32 changes on eight different occasions. Where did the information for those changes come from? From the public, who understood the ramifications of the budget but did not understand it in 11 days.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) reminds us of the little Dutch boy trying to plug one of the holes in the dike. What about all the other places where this government is hemorrhaging? When is this government going to act as quickly in all those other areas?
Members of Parliament, Mr. Speaker, have a .right to discuss legislation with their constituents. My constituents in Simcoe North are entitled to that opportunity when they see me on the weekend in Orillia, Midland, Penetanguishene, or on
a concession road. The Liberals have muzzled discussion, they are afraid of debate and do not want public opinion to interfere with their divine right of arrogance.
I want to read to the House the remarks of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) on December 7, 1981 when he spoke on a previous closure motion of this government. That champion of free speech said, as reported on page 13776 of Hansard:
-I have never objected to having any bills, and especially Bill C-48, being given detailed and attentive consideration by the members of this House.
That was the reason given for supporting closure. Where is that champion of freedom of speech now? His parliamentary secretary, who is in the House now, said as reported at page 13778 of Hansard:
During that period, the draft legislation has been subjected to most careful and detailed scrutiny which has surpassed that given to most legislation before this House.
Having made that statement, will that member stand in his place and speak against this motion? I wonder if today he will have the courage of his convictions which he had on that day and speak against this motion. We heard the President of the Treasury Board in what we might call his "we have heard" speech in which he spent a lot of time detailing the members who have spoken. Well, anyone can read that in Hansard. But no matter which opposition party debated the issue, no matter what the point of view of my colleagues to my left is, they have a right to bring forward their constituents' views. This government wants them to take two days, Saturday and Sunday, and come back here and try to express those views, and then it is going to shut them off.
We are concerned, Mr. Speaker, that the bill affects public servants unevenly. We are concerned about infringement on the collective bargaining process. We want to speak our minds and the minds of our constituents on this bill. But the Liberal government wants to cut off public debate, and that is wrong, wrong, wrong. My colleagues in this debate have elaborated at great and convincing length on the weaknesses of this bill. Therefore, I want to ask the question: Why did the government bring it in? Why did it bring such legislation before the people of Canada at this time? Well, Mr. Speaker, when 1 spoke in the budget debate I believed the government was doing this simply because public servants are a useful scapegoat in that they are a tenable and safe target politically.
Today on the front page of the newspaper we learn that the Liberals had access to a comprehensive survey that showed that public servants-and 1 regret this-are not held in equal esteem to working men and women in the private sector. To me, a man or woman who works in a federal hospital contributes just as much to the wellbeing of Canada as a man or woman who works on an automotive line in Oshawa. All of us in this Parliament should stand up for all workers equally. That is basic.
The cynicism of this government is such that it was able to take a comprehensive survey that said two things, and then write the bill from it. It said more than two, but two are relevant to this bill. One is that public servants are a safe political target. The second one is that the people of Canada understandably want some leadership. They have been without it for so long that we can understand that. Therefore, the Liberal government moved, quite cynically and quite hypocritically, knowing that controlling public servants' wages would not affect inflation one iota-maybe a slight iota but not very much at all-but simply to save their political hides in the short run. I want members of the Liberal Party to know that it is too late to do that. Their hides are gone. They will be gone in the next election from being the Government of Canada.
If that explains the cynicism and motives of the Liberals, I want to turn now, because my thoughts are of cynicism, to the activity of the Conservative Party. If anything, the cynicism portrayed by the government on this issue has been exceeded by that of the official opposition. The official opposition has walked on both sides of the street in the debate on wage

control legislation. The official opposition has done this right from day one. Just consider the record, Mr. Speaker.

I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the only party that can make those criticisms and vote for a bill that is unfair, that does nothing about prices, that discriminates against public servants and denies collective bargaining, is the Conservative Party of Canada.

speechtext: That is Tory logic.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext:
As my colleague says, it is Tory logic.
The cynicism has been compounded this afternoon by the first Tory speaker, the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis). He got to his feet and objected to closure. Isn't that sweet, Mr. Speaker? I think there has been a sweetheart deal between the Conservatives and the Liberals on this matter. The hon. member for Simcoe North got to his feet and said that we need more time to speak. That is another classical,

July 15, 1982
Time Allocation
hypocritical act. The Liberals are going to shut us up. But where have the Tories been for five days? In the past five days they have had the right to put up three times the number of speakers the New Democratic Party had. We had 12 members speak. The Progressive Conservative Party had only six. Where have they been? I will tell you where they have been, Mr. Speaker. They have been hiding. Out of one side of their mouths comes criticisms of the bill, trying to appeal to one part of the electorate, and out of the other side of their mouths comes support. 1 think the people of Canada before long will not only get on to the cynicism of the Liberal Party of Canada, the Liberal government, but also the people will be on to the outright cynicism of the opposition as well.
There is a fundamental issue at stake here. It is the faulty analysis of the Canadian economy which has led to the Government of Canada taking away the basic right of collective bargaining from the working people in this country. In that context, I think it is relevant in principle that in Poland it was recognized, and is recognized today, that there is an intrinsic connection between the notion itself and the right of people in their places of work, where they spend most of their lives, to have something called collective bargaining. It led to the most significant workers' movement since World War II. This took place in Europe, in Poland, whose people were committed to the notion of freedom.
I want to say that the parties in this House, the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party, paid wonderful lip service- I think it is more than lip service-to the right of people to have trade unions and to act freely as members of trade unions in Europe, and that if they are to have any integrity, they have to apply the same principle and the same sense of justice here in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: That absence of justice and that absence of fairness permeates this legislation, and we in this party will have nothing to do with it. Of course, because we have used our right to speak out against this bill and want to continue to do so, we in the New Democratic Party will oppose the closure motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in the budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has offered a very manageable target to help all Canadians beat inflation.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: Do we have to listen to this again?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: The Minister of Finance has said very clearly that 6 per cent should be a target for wages and prices, and that is a target well within everyone's grasp.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: Tell us why you have to have closure, then.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext:
The minister has made it very clear that he wants to build a world of 6 per cent which will create strength and genuine activity, that he wants to get rid of the world of 12
per cent that generates weakness, loss of jobs, loss of international trade and a continuing decline in our economy.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: Why have closure, then?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext:
We have set out a 6 per cent target in the budget because 6 per cent is a target that all of us can accomplish. It is most important we understand that simple idea. Six per cent is a world that we can all accomplish by working together. Six per cent is manageable, 6 per cent is strength and 6 per cent comes when Canadians co-operate together.
Today marks one of the key steps in the initial legislation to bring about a 6 per cent world. Today we are discussing a bill to restrain wage increases in the public service to a 6 per cent ceiling and then to a 5 per cent ceiling. We believe that that represents good leadership, good management and good savings for taxpayers.
First of all, it is good leadership because everyone in the public service is brought under this great umbrella; 500,000 of us are included in the 6 per cent-5 per cent world. It includes Members of Parliament, cabinet ministers, senators, senior executives, postal workers, people working for Air Canada and people working for every Crown corporation, every department and every branch of government. These 500,000 Canadians are included in this first effort toward a 6 per cent world. We have done that because these 500,000 people will provide leadership to the millions of other Canadians who daily make decisions which affect the economy. Through our action we are saying to people that we are prepared to limit our increases to an amount which will create health rather than weakness, a vital first step in the restoration of strength in our economy.
Second, the bill represents good management because $250 million will be saved this year alone and $550 million will be saved next year. Finally, it is a good use of these savings; it is a good reallocation of the $800 million which is being saved here. We are turning that back into our economy. We are turning it into jobs and into housing. We are turning it over to farmers and fishermen. We are turning it into grants for small businesses. We are asking people to create health by limiting their increases, and then we are using that money to generate health in vital sectors of our economy. This is the reason we introduced the bill. We want it for its leadership, for its good management, for the savings and stimulus it generates and, above all, as a symbol of co-operation and advancement in our economy.
Why are we worried about this? Why are we saying that 6 per cent is a manageable, desirable target? Why does the government constantly say that inflation must come down? We say it because inflation is the root disease in our economy. We do it because on the inside of our economy inflation is keeping our interest rates high, inflation is leading to greater unemployment and greater numbers of bankruptcies. Inflation has reached the point where it is creating weakness, and in turn
July 15, 1982

that weakness is creating further damage and further suffering. High interest rates are caused by inflation; high interest rates in turn create bankruptcies, and bankruptcies create unemployment. On the inside of our economy we must stop the disease which is weakening us before the weakness becomes permanent.
On the outside inflation is hurting us equally. On the outside inflation is pushing our prices too high. When the world economy recovers, we want to be there and to join in that recovery. We want the prices for the goods and the commodities we export to be competitive with those in other countries. For example, when the United States has a 6 per cent inflation rate, Canada cannot afford a 12 per cent one, or we will never again sell to the United States in the large quantities of the past.
The government has acted, and this bill is one of those actions. As I mentioned earlier, this bill is a threefold effort. It provides leadership, good management and vital stimulus. It underlines our main message that we must get inflation down and create a 6 per cent growth level. We cannot afford to do that by picking out single people or single groups in society and making them scapegoats. We have heard from our close friends in the New Democratic Party the vital message that we must be careful, that we cannot pick out single groups. They are right about that, but they are wrong to assume that the 6 per cent battle will stop with public servants. The 6 per cent battle must go all through the economy. It must include executives, private businessmen and wage earners in the private sector.
Many of these people are already making sacrifices. I know, because I own my own business and I know the types of problems which inflation and tough times are creating for my business, that businessmen today are making sacrifices. We are asking our associates in the private sector to join with us in making equal sacrifices. We are not seeking our scapegoats. If we all ask for inflation minus a little bit, then for a short time we may all have to sacrifice, but in the long run we will certainly all gain from a stronger economy and from a greater, more vigorous ability to export abroad.
Those are the points behind this legislation-the point that we are in this together, the point that we are prepared to make small sacrifices, and the point that a 6 per cent world is a much stronger, much healthier and much more vigorous place than a 12 per cent world of inflation and weakness. We are aiming for 6 per cent, and we are aiming for that strength.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that we have to speak again to a closure motion. I understand that the government introduced this motion because it felt the New Democratic Party was filibustering the debate and carrying it on for too long.
I do not think it would surprise any member of the House if I say that I am not very often in agreement with members of the NDP. Perhaps their diagnosis is all right, but their cure is worse than the disease. But I defend the right of the New Democratic Party, its leader, Dennis McDermott, and its deputy leader, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), to present their views. It is their democratic right to speak, just
Time Allocation
as that is the right of any member of the House. I may not agree with what they have to say, especially when it comes to the solutions which they offer the country.
Their idea of a solution is that if a patient has cancer, kill the patient rather than perform surgery. Nevertheless, I agree that they should be able to speak. I think it helps us all when they speak as much as they can, because every time they speak they help us. This is particularly the case when the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) speaks and The Vancouver Sun publishes his speeches. It ensures that the former hon. member for Kootenay West will return to the House. I encourage liberal and free debate in the House and giving members of the NDP a free rein to speak as long as they wish. Thus, I oppose the closure motion.
I say sincerely that the government wants closure because the legislation before us is very pockmarked. It has many flaws in it. There are many reasons people think it deserves real examination. There are unfair elements in it which ought to be exposed. I think the government is afraid that extensive debate will expose the weaknesses in the legislation. In fact, there is so much hypocrisy in the government's proposal to restrain wages that it does not want to have extensive debate on the matter.
This reminds me of the scenario four years ago when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) travelled to Europe and met with the Chancellor of West Germany. He returned with a marvellous restraint program at the beginning of August. He obtained free television time to announce a new program of restraint. We had finished one just two years previous to that. That was the time when just before the government announced the restraint program he carpeted the dining room upstairs and provided new silverware. In August, 1978 the Prime Minister announced another restraint program. Since then the debt of this country has been escalating.
The hypocrisy of this program is that while it may save the government approximately $200 million this year, as the parliamentary secretary just said, it will have absolutely no bearing on the spending program of the government. Restraint is being carried on the backs of the workers. As we heard in question period today and yesterday, the government is asking public servants to carry a 6 per cent load, but it can increase the prices of its services anywhere from 20 per cent to 50 per cent. It seems to me that if we are to look at all at the principle of fairness, the government ought to impose a 6 per cent increase on the prices that it charges the public if it is asking the public service to carry a 6 per cent load.
I find this worrisome. I am concerned about the fact that there is this sudden and almost cataclysmic turn of events in Canada. I, and I am sure all members, recall last year when the country was subjected to a six-week postal strike. I remember talking to my constituents who were small-business men and paying $3,000 a month to have their accounts receivable statements delivered. This was on the verge of putting some of those small businesses under. After six weeks the government

July 15, 1982
Time Allocation
settled for almost the same amount that was on the bargaining table when the strike began. The settlement was at a percentage far in excess of the 6 per cent level which we are looking at now. I am saying to the government that if they are such good managers, where were they a year ago when it was looking at percentage increases?
The government is also talking about productivity. A year ago, along with that postal price increase, it was negotiating for a 17-week period of maternity leave at which time there is no productivity on the job. Where was the government a year ago? Did it not have enough foresight to plan for the crunch that was coming a year later or to see that it would be in a deficit position? Instead of a $10.5 billion deficit, could it not see that we would have a $20.5 billion debt? A year ago the government settled far in excess of the 6 per cent limit which it is now imposing. Where are these great government planners, which they tend to think they are?
The parliamentary secretary said that the cost of government and the cost of production has escalated because of inflation and we therefore must bring inflation down. I do not argue with that. I now notice that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) is deflecting that particular argument. I noted with particular interest yesterday that the Minister of Finance, when answering a question by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), said as reported at page 19315 of Hansard of July 14, 1982:
Has he stopped to ask himself what is the cause of high interest rates? ... My answer to that question is high prices. Until we get our rate of inflation down, do not ask for relief on the interest rate front.
Now we suddenly get this new economic theory which says that the cost of inflation comes from high prices. It is a truism of this government that it will blame everyone else but itself. Now it is blaming the merchandisers and the consumers. It is blaming the business community for the high prices and the high cost of living. Never mind that approximately $40 billion of government debts will come due next year. Never mind that in order to renew those debts the inflationary costs of the government will spiral.
Third, we have to examine this legislation because of the inherent unfairness within it in two areas. It is unfair in the first instance because it is based on a percentage increase. I remember when I was a member of the IWA working at Fraser Mills years ago. I wondered then about the legitimacy of asking for wage increases based on percentages. In those days I was working for 95 cents or $1 an hour. I was to receive a 5 per cent or 6 per cent increase while the foremen, on a percentage increase basis, were going to get considerably more. I admit that the foremen have a responsibility that deserves more pay, but if we consider the rollbacks under this legislation it will mean that the deputy ministers will have a substantial amount of money left over for their disposable incomes but those who are janitors in local government buildings will have precious little left over in their disposable income.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: Vote against the bill then.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext:
What is also eminently unfair in this legislation is that it does not provide for any discussion or negotiations of any union contract concerning matters of other than a fiscal nature. It seems to me that in order to preserve the right of collective bargaining, this bill should make negotiations of that type possible so as to ensure that the right to collective bargaining remains in every union agreement.
If the government wants to put a ceiling on wages, that is its business. However, in order to preserve fairness in the labour market and a favourable working climate where there is an atmosphere of conciliation and understanding, the government must make provision in this bill to allow for negotiation of nonfiscal matters such as health in the workplace, safety in the workplace and all those other areas which do not concern financial matters.
Another shortcoming of this bill is that it does not cover non-unionized workers. It is fine for the NDP to speak on behalf of the UAW and all those strong unions, but who will speak for the workers who are non-unionized? Who speaks on behalf of the weak? Six per cent of nothing is nothing.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: Certainly not the Tories.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext:
This bill will do nothing for the 1.3 million unemployed. Therefore, I oppose the government's move to impose closure on us. We need the freedom to speak even though we, within the confines of this chamber, may not always agree.

speakeroldname: Mr. Henri Tousignant (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief, since I think this debate has gone on long enough. I was pleased when the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) proposed a motion to limit the debate.
As hon. members are aware, we have been discussing this bill for four days, and the debate has given rise to all kinds of comments, especially by members of the New Democratic Party. Mr. Speaker, it is just unbelievable, all the contradictions, all the nonsense we have had to listen to here in this House. It goes to show, Mr. Speaker, that it is about time the House adjourned for the summer recess. My colleague from Kitchener (Mr. Lang) commented earlier that there was nothing worse for a person's health than listening to the members opposite. I must say I am so astonished at the kind of nonsense I hear at times that I have to pinch myself to make sure I am in the real world. Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am not so sure I am in the real world because, outside Parliament, I was used to people who managed to earn a living without wasting other people's time. The comments we have had to listen to! These members are up in arms about high interest rates, they are up in arms about the excessively high cost of housing, food and clothing, and the high rate of inflation, and so forth, and on
July 15, 1982

the other hand, they are squarely opposed to the measure that will help bring down inflation.
As I implied at the outset, Mr. Speaker, I am shocked. I think it is outrageous the way these people are carrying on. They remind me of hunting dogs who start barking when they manage to corner a deer and start moving in for the kill.
In any event, one does not need a degree in economics to analyse the present situation. The problem facing us all in Canada right now is, of course, inflation. There are people who prefer to ignore this fact and let others worry about it, but inflation, Mr. Speaker, is something that makes us think about our own habits and those of all Canadians. We have had fat years, and we took advantage of them, and in doing so, we may have gone somewhat overboard. Not just the workers. Often people tend to blame labour and the unions, but it is not just the workers, everyone is involved, including employers, business people and industrialists who started living the good life and spending a bit more on luxuries. For instance, a travelling salesman instead of trying to bargain a little and get a room for $35 or $40-those prices still exist-will take the most expensive room, at $75 or $80. He spends the whole evening at the bar and all this goes on his company's expense account. The company makes everyone pay, including the consumer. That is life, but again, that is inflation. It is as simple as that.
Einstein said that great minds have always been violently opposed by mediocre intellects. So we might as well ignore people who are trying to intervene in this debate. Mr. Speaker, we, on the government side, wanted to take action in areas that are our concern. People are fond of saying that the Canadian government is always interfering in matters that are none of its business. For once it is our business, namely, the public service. This is no punitive measure, and we have nothing against these people. In fact, they are our allies, these are people we work with regularly, people we see every day, people who help us.
So, what is actually going on right now? I think we can agree that inflation exists, and when people complain that the cost of housing and food and other commodities is too high, this is often due to excessive wage demands on the part of various groups, demands made by business, and so forth, as I mentioned earlier. So if we agree that inflation exists and is going to be with us for some time, what do we do to fight inflation? There is a price, if we want to bring inflation down to more reasonable levels. Right now, who is paying the price for bringing inflation within more normal proportions? That price is being paid by the last workers to be hired on the assembly line, who are also the first to be fired and to join the ranks of the unemployed. These are the people who are paying that price today.
The members opposite who are criticizing belong to the unemployment party, because they are promoting this kind of unemployment. They do not want to give others a chance to make a life for themselves. So who is paying the price? First of
Time Allocation
all, the unemployed, who are being laid off because of the general economic slowdown. Businessmen and merchants, who any day may lose everything they own because of high interest rates, are also among those who are paying the price of bringing inflation down to normal levels. However, we also have a group of people whose jobs are safe, and we are telling them: Well, you have a safe job and on top of that, we are going to give you an extra bonus so that you can walk all over the people who are making sacrifices today, namely the unemployed and the businessman who is in danger of losing his business. That is what we are doing, and it does not make sense.
A few moments ago I heard someone say: It is unfair, it is unfair! Yes it is unfair, I agree. Mr. Speaker, if I were a civil servant and I were earning $15,000 a year, I would prefer to go without a raise rather than losing my job or living on welfare. The choice is obvious. What we want to do now with the 6 per cent rule, starting with our own group, is to set an example, and if the Canadian public approves, and this is not even ... Yes, 1 realize my time is running out, Mr. Speaker, I am going to finish. If Canadians would agree to lower their expectations somewhat, we would be able to ride out this recession, which would be only temporary, but on the other hand, if Canadians refuse, it is going to get worse. Often, people like to compare Canada with the United States, and they wonder why, if we are both applying the same monetary policy, the inflation rate in the United States is going down. We must understand that the United States is a free enterprise country and is not as compartmentalized and regulated, planned and controlled as ours. One example that illustrates this is that workers in the automotive industry agreed to a wage reduction. Here, we have no room for manoeuvre and that is why everything is stratified and compartmentalized. That is why our inflation rate is not going down at the same rate. However, if interest rates were to go down, obviously, inflation would be less severe. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, since my time has almost expired, I would like to inform the House that I am very pleased that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) has asked to end this debate, and I hope that all our hon. colleagues will support the measure we have just imposed.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are now dealing with another example of this government's ability not only to muzzle the opposition but the Canadian public. Our desire was to bring this bill to committee where it would receive total exposure, be reviewed and assessed and we could get the view of the public.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: That is committee, not second reading.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: Will it ever get to committee?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board

speechtext:
We are wondering that too.

July 15, 1982
