subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext:
Instead of backbenchers continuing to defend the position of the government, I wish one day they would stand up and answer to the public who are concerned about losing their jobs, not worrying about civil servants getting a 6 per cent raise in pay. This bill would not have been necessary if this government had not destroyed the economy over the past 14 years.
I would like to quote from the original architect that the Liberal government used. John Kenneth Galbraith has finally admitted it all: "Economists make predictions, not because they know, but because they are asked." Is that not great? There we have the answer about the Liberal policy that put this country on its knees, as it is today. Those are the kind of people the Liberals have attracted to draw up their policy, to bring three budgets forward that have all been destructive to this country. He was the man who started in 1968 giving them their answers. They asked the questions: he gave the answers. He is admitting now that they were not very good answers.
It is the socialist rhetoric of John Kenneth Galbraith and his type that has destroyed the middle class Canadian, those who were born with the thought that at some time they could own a home at a reasonable price. They are now paying exhorbitant interest rates, through exorbitant inflation, meaning an exorbitant cost for the house.
Let us look at this bill. The government referred to this as restraint. If this were restraint in the pure sense-that is, real restraint-yes, I could solidly support it. But how can I support this bill as restraint?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: You are going to support it.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext:
It does nothing more than guarantee that every member in this House, every civil servant in Ottawa, and every federal civil servant around the country will get a 6 per cent increase in pay. We have very close to a million and a half people unemployed and they are not impressed with the fact that we have protected ourselves by this 6 per cent increase in pay. What should have been brought in as restraint is a 10 per cent cut on every budget across the board. We should have taken a 10 per cent cut in our pay-or at least work towards that over the next three years. This is too little, too late.
We requested that a parliamentary committee be set up to review all the estimates, to look at the loopholes, to find out where we could cut back on some of the programs not needed right now.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: You had an opportunity.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext:
We have not had an opportunity because we have been refused by the government that has put us in the place we are today. All the government comes up with is patchwork solutions, and patchwork solutions do not solve a major structural problem. It is like taking a car which has been in an accident, trying to bend the frame into the right position, and then telling the owner that that car is in good order. Everyone in this House knows that once the frame of a car is
bent it is destroyed, it is of no value. That is the problem with our economy.
Yesterday, I spent a very interesting afternoon. The leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) and myself were in the region of Durham before the regional councillors. Many of those people who run a very important region of this country asked us to come because they are concerned. The first point they brought out was their concern over the current monetary policy which has produced and maintained high interest rates, causing enormous economic hardships to consumers and corporations alike. Those people who are responsible for the municipality, representing all the mayors of that area, wanted to hear from us as to what was really happening in Ottawa. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, I wish the Liberals had been there. I wish that the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove), who happens to be my buddy in that area, had been there to represent the government.
There are many points that the leader of the New Democratic Party and myself agreed on. We agreed on lower interest rates but we did not agree on the method of getting there. We agreed to support the samll-business man and get the economy going. What we were saying yesterday was that the government is bringing in Bill C-124, it provides a 6 per cent increase in pay, but they have not talked about any reduction in their expenditure. Those councillors are concerned. They are concerned about our unrestricted imports. We have done absolutely nothing, Mr. Speaker, to encourage the private sector to produce, in order to replace such imports. Our dollar is low enough now. If there were a tax incentive there, we could be starting new industries and creating jobs, and that is the name of the game.
We are guaranteeing the civil service that they will have their jobs, plus a 6 per cent increase in pay, but we are doing nothing for the rest of Canada.
This government has destroyed all the incentives of the private sector. They have removed all incentive to foreign investment. This is a very large country. It requires large sums of money. Admittedly, today Canadians are saving large sums of money, but Canadians historically have kept their money in their socks. The foreign investors have put money into industry. I maintain that foreign investment review itself is not working and has helped destroy our credibility in international markets.
We should be going out to encourage European investors and Japanese investors to come into our country. We should be encouraging the Japanese to produce cars here. But they do not know what the position will be like here in six or seven months; they think that we may say: "We do not want you any more, so get your plants out of Canada". Incentives are required, Mr. Speaker, not grants. We need incentives to get Canadian dollars out of the banks and into industry.
The National Energy Program was a total destruction of the Canadian oil industry. Today there are 50 per cent less drilling rigs operating than there were last year at the same time.
July 15, 1982

We have been criticized many times for our mortgage interest deductibility proposal. Would that not have assisted the Canadian public, would it not have assisted the banks? They would have repossessed half the houses, because people would have been able to keep up mortgage payments. That plan would have assisted our general construction economy. We have done nothing but talk about a 6 per cent increase in pay for the civil service next year. That is why we want this bill put into committee over an extended period of time so that we can hear witnesses from across the country.
This budget is like every other budget that the government has brought forward. There is absolutely no foresight and they are too frightened to take hindsight because they look at the morass that they have left behind. This government, in my opinion, is carrying out a financial scam on the Canadian public and it should be stopped. It is time the public had the choice to decide whether they want this government to stay any longer or not.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had some discussion today about the time allocation which is being proposed for this bill. I want to touch on that matter for a moment before turning to the substance of the question before us in Bill C-124.
Quite obviously there is a need to limit debate on matters before the House. We cannot continue to consider issues indefinitely here, especially when opportunities await members to consider the same matters in committee. When we hear allegations of muzzling Parliament or muzzling the opposition, I wonder whether members opposite have considered the British practices which do in fact place real limitations on the time taken for debates in the British House of Commons. I wonder whether hon. members opposite would not find those precedents instructive for our own practices here in Ottawa.
1 hope usefully that the committee currently studying the proposed modifications to our procedures will look at that particular precedent so that all hon. members might be assured that our business can deal with more effectively. Through more self-discipline, we could limit the time that we spend on debates here in the House to the benefit of all.
In the specific case of Bill C-124 now before us, we have had extensive debate involving a substantial number of members. The subject matter will, of course, go to committee where there will be further consideration, and there will be another opportunity to speak about the bill when it returns from the committee to the House.
With respect to the substance of the bill, we have heard allegations, particularly today by the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), that somehow the wage restraint program being introduced for the public service for the next two years will neither create jobs nor reduce inflation. It is remarkable that an hon. member would make such a statement, when he and others must know perfectly well that until such time as we
Time Allocation
succeed in limiting inflation we shall not be able to create more jobs nor reduce interest rates. Why do I say that? It is evident that wage increases in Canada in recent years have consistently run at levels higher than those in most of our major trade competitors. Canada is heavily dependent on world trade for its prosperity. Foreign trade amounts to 30 per cent of our gross national product, and of that 30 per cent, some 70 per cent is trade with the United States.
What has been the wage situation in the United States, our major trading partner? During 1981 wage settlements in the United States were, on average, some four percentage points lower than in Canada. That means significant competitive advantage for United States industries over comparable Canadian industries which have had wage increases at a level of about 12 per cent, on average, during the last year.
Not only were average wage settlements in the United States lower than in Canada during 1981, but in the first quarter of this year United States increases in industrial wages for the first year of labour contracts averaged only 2.2 per cent. The Teamsters and the UAW, two major unions in the United States, accepted a complete freeze on wages, so that even if one extracted those two elements, the average in the United States was still only 6.8 per cent during the first quarter of this year, whereas increases in Canada have been running typically at about 12 per cent. I might also note that in the United States public service increases of only 4.8 per cent have been provided for in 1982, in contrast with the 6 per cent level that is envisaged in the legislation now before us.
I do not think it takes any great expertise in economics to understand that with such a wage situation in a highly competitive trade world, Canada is placing itself at a disadvantage.
It is not just that wage restraint in Canada is an essential part of any anti-inflationary policy; it is also evident that over the longer term Canadian industry will be unable to compete in world markets if our wage levels consistently exceed those of our main competitors and, indeed, if those wage settlements consistently exceed productivity increases here in Canada.
Unfortunately, we have had a situation in recent years in which our increases in productivity have been significantly lower than those of our major trade competitors. It is an oversimplification, of course, to argue that the main reason for a drop in productivity in Canada or for slower productivity increases is entirely ascribable to high wage settlements. There are other major factors which also cause productivity changes in any industrial economy. However, it remains true, nevertheless, that when wage level increases in Canada consistently outstrip increases in productivity, it must be that more inflation will result, and it must be that Canada will become increasingly less competitive in world markets.
Against that background, if we really want to help Canadians by setting a standard for the whole of the Canadian economy, it is essential that this legislation pass quickly. If pay

July 15, 1982
Time Allocation
increases are not restrained, we shall not be competitive. We shall not address a major factor in our inflation equation. We shall find ourselves faced with continuing high interest rates and high unemployment.
1 do not know that hon. members opposite, particularly members of the New Democratic Party, have accepted the fact that there is a pressing need for the federal government to set a standard, to set an example for the rest of the major players in the Canadian economy. Prior to the budget of a fortnight ago, we saw that the business community-there were some exceptions but broadly speaking-called for voluntary wage controls rather than mandatory controls. The business community resisted suggestions from various quarters for a sweeping program of mandatory wage and price controls-although some businessmen advocated such a policy-and called instead, for example, through the Business Council on National Issues, for a voluntary program. That voluntary program is now available for them to take up. The opportunity is there. They have said that they want it. The time has now come for them to respond.
The government is providing leadership. The government has said, in the case of its own more than half a million employees, that it will show restraint. The government has said that it will ensure that public service wages will not contribute, as they have in the past, to mounting rates of inflation in our country. It is now for the business community-which wanted voluntary controls-to take this opportunity.
The government is providing leadership; now let the business community respond. Equally, the provinces and municipalities must respond. They must bring forward their own programs of restraint in order to ensure that inflation is not again fueled by excessive wage settlements in either our public sector or our private sector. The situation in Canada has been well stated by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) who, toward the end of last month, stated the following in a speech:
Businessmen, although preaching restraint, often found it simpler to give in to excessive wage demands. In the inflationary environment which developed, it was possible for them, until recently, to recoup higher wage costs by raising the prices of their products. Productivity, once of highest priority, slipped well down the list of goals.
That situation in Canada must now change. The government has provided a new sense of direction and a new leadership. For my part, I do not doubt that the private sector will respond, that the provinces will respond, that the municipalities will respond and, indeed, that we shall see a world where 6 per cent wage settlements for the next 12 months and 5 per cent for the following 12 months will help to provide the necessary conditions for our economic recovery.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like my colleagues I am somewhat distressed to have to rise once again to oppose a Liberal government motion enforcing closure. In this case it cuts off debate on Bill C-124 respecting compensation in the public service. What is printed in this bill is important, so is what is left out of it and what is left unexplained.
Firstly, I wish to speak of the plight of the old age pensioners; then I wish to say a few words about the Armed Forces pensioners. In the Minister of Finance's budget speech he mentioned the pay limits encompassed in this bill and also the capping of the indexing of pensions for old age pensioners and public servants. He did so in these words:
Effective January 1, 1983, indexation of the pensions paid to former Members of Parliament and public servants will be limited to 6 per cent. The indexing factor will be lowered to 5 per cent as of January 1, 1984.
Effective the same dates, the indexing factor applicable to family allowances and old age security will also be limited to 6 per cent and 5 per cent.
This capping of indexation, Mr. Speaker, is particularly devastating to those old age pensioners who have made some provision by themselves to look after themselves in their old age. The budget singles out for the harshest treatment those pensioners who saved and paid into various private pensions. The payment of the usual indexation on old age security only to those who are also drawing the guaranteed income supplement is a direct disincentive for anyone to try and make plans for enjoying their old age in part on their own resources. Anyone now working and saving for a private pension, annuity or RRSP will now realize that they will be discriminated against by this government and only the portion of their private plan which exceeds the value of the guaranteed income supplement will be of any value to them. Anyone with a private pension, annuity or insurance benefit which gives them something under $240 a month has simply reduced his or her guaranteed income supplement by that amount. The government should not be surprised to find that the steady growth over the years in the percentage of old age pensioners who have qualified for the GIS will now accelerate. The government has provided an additional incentive for senior citizens to arrange their affairs so that they get on GIS. It is the only way their basic pension will keep up with inflation rates.
I have an example which might cause the government to think about this if it were not in such a hurry to force legislation through this House by closure. In Victoria there are two large apartment buildings known as the Lord and Lady Simcoe on Simcoe Street. They house about 270 tenants, almost all of whom are retired and over half of which are widows. It is estimated that only some ten or 20 people in these buildings are still in the work force. The rest are retired and they are truly the fixed income people that one hears about here. On June 9 those tenants received notice of a rent increase. I know rent controls are in the purview of provincial governments but these cases might help illustrate to this unheeding and unfeeling government just what the people out there in the real world face, and the importance of a fair deal on indexation of their pensions.
As you may or may not be aware, Mr. Speaker, there are three categories of rent control in B.C. You can be exempt from rent control on certain types of accommodation- generally public or high priced accommodation-or you can have rent review, which is not nearly as favourable a position to be in if you are renting. The third category is units under
July 15, 1982

rent control where the landlord has to have permission before he can raise your rent. All 270 of the units in this complex I am speaking of are in the second category.
I have in my hand a notice given to a couple in a two-bedroom suite. They tell me that when they rented their suite seven years ago it was $220 a month. It was raised by the allowable limit each year for several years, and last year the landlord managed to increase rents by 15 per cent which put it over the $350 a month limit, thereby taking it out of the rent control area into the rent review area. The current rent for this particular couple is $424 a month, with an increase coming of $98 a month. Therefore, they will soon start paying $522 a month, an increase of 23 per cent. This is what happens to people out in the real world.
I heard the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Tousig-nant) say that people are being asked to go without a few little luxuries. That is not what is happening; these people are being asked to pay an additional 23 per cent rent on their suites. A great number of them are going to have leave their suites, which they have lived in for years,'and move into rooms in houses. This is not a little luxury for those people, believe me.
I wish to turn now, Mr. Speaker, to another aspect of this capping of indexation which is not mentioned in the bill but should be because of doubt out there about what is going to happen to the people involved. It has to do with the application of the 85 rule. That rule means a retired serviceman will not start to get his pension indexed until his age plus years of service totals 85. It also applies to civil servants but because of different retirement ages it is difficult to talk about the two groups at the same time. Some people have to wait for years to reach that point.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, as a non-lawyer I would inquire about the legality of what the government is planning to do to long service annuitants. The Armed Forces, when serving, pay an additional 1.5 per cent of their pay into the pension fund to cover the cost of indexing. This has always been considered part of their contract. Now, apparently, it is not to be honoured after next January.
As a background to this action the government should bear in mind that the Canadian forces' superannuation account, plus their actuarial liability account, as of March 31, 1981 was over $9 billion. This information comes from the answer to a question I put on the Order Paper. The government has this $9 billion, an increase of $1.2 billion over the preceding two years, and it borrows this money-a paper transaction-at a rate of 2.15 per cent per quarter, which is 8.6 per cent per annum. A very cheap source of money for the government. Yet the government is now prepared to break its contract to index the pension of retired servicemen.
The reason I bring it up at this time is that it is not in the bill and servicemen are wondering what is going to happen. Some of them retired ten years ago and have not yet reached the 85 rule point. When they reach that status they would receive the cost of living increases from the preceding years; not in a lump sum, but they would have gone to the level of purchasing power they had when they retired. They are now wondering what is going to happen. If it is going to be 11 per
Time Allocation
cent this year, will they get that 11 per cent? Will it be 6 per cent? What will it be next year? No one knows, and the government should not leave these people in such doubt.
Those are the unanswered questions about this bill, Mr. Speaker, and they should be answered before the government gags Parliament on such an important piece of legislation. I realize it is going to committee and that will be a great place to talk about it. But I am worried that so many of the government's bills are rushed into committee nowadays. I suspect the reason is that there is a greater audience for the debates in this chamber, thanks to the electronic age, than there is for what goes on in committee. We all know that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank my colleague opposite. I only hope that I can count on his co-operation as we debate this particular motion and, indeed, the entire bill, C-124. Six per cent co-operation would be very helpful. That is all we are asking for in Bill C-124.
I had the opportunity to speak on second reading of this bill the other night so I am not going to go into all the details again.
I should like to comment on some of the things that have been mentioned this afternoon regarding the motion to limit debate. The word "closure" and other terms have been used. Mr. Speaker, there comes a time when all that needs to be said has been said. If we were hearing anything new, it would be different. The government has a responsibility to provide legislation and to run the business affairs of Parliament and of the country. We should get on with curing the economic ills of the country. Bill C-124 is the instrument to bring down inflation which, of course, will result in interest rates coming down and in a reduction in the federal deficit. The entire economic future of the nation is based on Bill C-124.
If hon. members opposite are serious when they speak about the economic ills of the day and about offering cures for them, then I am surprised at their attitude and especially at the official opposition, which announced earlier today that it will vote against the motion. If something new were being said on Bill C-124 or suggestions were being put forward to cure the economic ills of the day, that would be a different matter. There comes a time when we have to get on with running the affairs of the country whether hon. members like it or not, and that is the responsibility of the party in power which sits on this side of the House.
The hon. member for Etobicoke North (Mr. MacLaren) spoke about parliamentary reform. I hope that the special committee set up to look into that matter during the summer will examine the delaying tactics that occur day in and day out in this House which prevent legislation from going through. Often members on both sides of the House agree on the basic intent of many bills, but whether to score political points in their constituencies or for whatever reason, hon. members opposite delay, delay, delay. Many more members of the

July 15, 1982
Time Allocation
opposition have spoken on Bill C-124 than members on this side of the House. Of course, their main purpose was to criticize. There has been plenty of opportunity to debate the bill. Our main purpose in this House should be to bring inflation down.
Just the other night I said that federal civil servants could be the heroes of the day through their involvement in this wage restraint program. 1 have heard from a number of them who say that they feel they will be, and indeed are, the front runners in this matter of wage restraint and the battle against inflation. I have heard from constituents who said the same thing. We know that business leaders and many labour leaders agree that something has to be done and that this bill is a step in the right direction.
We should get on with the business of passing the bill, Mr. Speaker. We know very well that it will be debated fully in committee where there will be plenty of time for argument and suggestions and perhaps for amendments as well. I am sure that witnesses will be heard in committee and that there will be plenty of time to bring out the full facts. The bill will come back to the House then for further debate. I do not know why hon. members opposite are so upset because we are trying to cure the economic ills of the day by getting the bill through.
There are other pieces of legislation which should be passed before this session ends, Mr. Speaker. On this side of the House we have been trying to get the bill through to aid home owners who have problems with urea formaldehyde foam insulation. The bill would provide compensation for them and 1 would not like to see Parliament adjourn for the summer without seeing that bill passed; but if we are going to have these delaying tactics day in and day out, then we are not going to get to that very important bill. I think that is a duty and responsibility that all members of the House should keep in mind.
The basic premise of Bill C-124 is to bring inflation down to 6 per cent and 5 per cent over the next two years. All that is being asked is that the federal civil servants and employees of Crown corporations, federally regulated agencies and the like be limited to 6 and 5 per cent wage increases-not decreases. The money saved by this measure will be devoted to much needed job-creation programs. Hon. members opposite fail to bring that point out; nearly $1 billion will be available for job-creation programs which are badly needed.
This afternoon the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) mentioned that a recent Gallup poll shows that 80 per cent of Canadians would sooner take a 10 per cent cut in pay than be unemployed, so the Canadian public in general is behind this bill. We should get on with it so that we can create those jobs and make money available to help the housing industry, for instance. Many questions are raised about the lack of housing, yet through this bill we are trying to get the money to provide houses so that young people will be in a position to own their own homes.
Basically, I see nothing wrong with limiting debate on this bill. Everything that needs to be said has been said. The bill will be debated further in committee and then brought back to the House and then, we hope, will be passed so that we can go on to cure the economic ills of the day. All that we are asking is 6 per cent and 5 per cent. As hon. members know, members of the House are also going to be involved.
All across the country people are crying for leadership and action. This is one area in which Parliament can provide action and leadership, but it must come from both sides of the House. We have an opportunity to show that leadership by passing Bill C-124. There is no reason why debate should not be limited and I shall certainly vote in favour of the motion, Mr. Speaker.

THE GRAND LODGE OF THE BENEVOLENT AND PROTECTIVE ORDER OF ELKS OF THE DOMINION OF CANADA
speechtext:
that Bill S-27, to amend the act of incorporation of The Grand Lodge of the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks of the Dominion of Canada, be read the second time and, by unanimous consent, referred to a Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, there were no comments made on Bill S-27 at first reading. There has been an agreement among the parties that we will each make a brief statement and then we will deal with the other stages of the bill without debate.
1 am pleased to sponsor Bill S-27 on behalf of The Grand Lodge of the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks of the Dominion of Canada. At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I want to extend my own appreciation to the House leaders and members on both sides of the House for their co-operation in allowing this bill to be debated today at second reading, in Committee of the Whole and third reading in one sitting. It is not controversial and it is a very worthy bill. It is one that means a great deal to many people across the country, namely, members of the Elks themselves and many thousands of people across Canada whom they help.
The purpose of the legislation in question and now before Parliament is to remove the restriction limiting at $100,000 the value of real property which might be acquired by the society or any of its branches. This restriction was incorporated into the act in 1913. In view of the increase in prices generally and of land in particular since that date, it is no longer realistic. Indeed, the origins of the restriction are not entirely clear, although it seems to have been the practice to place such restrictions on branch holdings of other societies incorporated by Parliament at that particular time.
The second purpose of the bill is to enable the society to change its head office from place to place, if necessary.
The third purpose is to substitute a French name for the English name of the society which appeared in the long title of the French version of the original act of incorporation. In this connection there is a further consequential amendment.
Finally, I am advised that the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks of the Dominion of Canada now has 360 lodges established in every province of Canada. They have 61,000 members, plus an additional 17,000 members of its ladies' auxiliary.
I am sure that all hon. members of the Parliament of Canada join in wishing the Elks every success in all their very fine work wherever they may live in Canada.

speechtext:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House a copy of the latest signed agreement between the government and the province of Quebec under the Canada Assistance Plan.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think my first remark should be to clear what may be a point of misunderstanding since just recently reference was made to what happened last Friday. I should like to put on the record that the only conversation I had prior to four o'clock on Friday afternoon was with a representative of the New Democratic Party. It was not in order to seek any agreement whatsoever; it was purely clarification of the subject matter which was to be discussed. That was the total extent of the conversation. In other words, there were no discussions of which I was aware between any members on this side and any members on the other side as to the subsequent procedures which were adopted by unanimous consent of the members present.
I think it is important to make that point because there was the inference of some sort of collusion or something of the sort. I certainly was not aware of that. In fact, I publicly express my surprise, but my pleasure nevertheless, at the turn of events on Friday.
The subject this afternoon is the Canada Assistance Plan, a subject which I hold dear to my heart. I have used the request for documents passing between the government and the province of Quebec under the Canada Assistance Plan as the vehicle for this discussion.
I requested these documents, as I have requested the documents applicable to the other provinces, as a result of discussions which took place in the hearings held last spring by the special committee which was formed to look at fiscal transfer payments. We criss-crossed the country and heard a plea from
Canada Assistance Plan
many social service groups that these documents should be available to them.
It may be somewhat ironic that we discussed the freedom of information act at great length and yet documents which are vital to the interest of people on social welfare and receiving social services are not available to the groups who are responsible for the provision of these services. It may be of interest to some members if I refer to an answer I received over a year ago as to the reasons why such documents were not being made available to the public in general. An official from the Department of National Health and Welfare said that in his opinion the province of Ontario, in this case, could and probably would object because that would facilitate their municipalities making interprovincial comparisons. He said that this was, of course, assuming that the schedules for the other provinces were also released. He indicated that such a comparison would lead to whipsawing from one province to another. He also made an interesting comment at that time, which is quite applicable now, that under the proposed free-' dom of information act items which would be detrimental to federal-provincial relations can be exempted from release.
Personally, I do not see any reason why the groups that are responsible for social services in the different provinces should not be able to make comparisons from province to province and should not, as a result, be able to pressure their respective provincial governments into giving them the same services which they see being made available to persons in need in the other provinces.
I have several objections to the way that the Canada Assistance Plan presently operates. At the outset, let me say that this has nothing to do with the total funding. I have said before in the House and I will repeat that I firmly believe in the maximum possible funding at the federal level. I say that because under those circumstances the distribution of those funds from the federal treasury should go to the provinces on an equitable basis, and the raising of those funds at the federal level means that the moneys are raised from those provinces which are the best able to pay.
However, it does not work out this way in the case of the Canada Assistance Plan. I have some figures to illustrate this. For example, let us take my own province of Quebec which is the one referred to in the motion. According to the latest year for which figures are available, the province of Quebec received 39 per cent of the funding under the Canada Assistance Plan, and as you are aware, Mr. Speaker, it has 26 per cent of the population of this country.
There is probably good reason why Quebec, with its greater number of persons in need, should receive a larger share. However, let us look at another province which is also in need. Nova Scotia. Incidentally, the Premier of that province, as late as a few days ago, was bitterly complaining that the federal government was decreasing its transfers to the provinces and making life difficult for the province of Nova Scotia. I read that particular lie in today's Globe and Mail, that the federal government was cutting its funding for post-secondary education and health services. I say "lie" because anyone who looks

July 15, 1982
19378_______________________________________
Canada Assistance Plan
at the figures is aware that the federal funding for both postsecondary education and health services is increased this year and increased substantially. Elowever, one also understands that in difficult times the provision of social services becomes an increasingly hard load for provinces like Nova Scotia which have an increasing number of unemployed and persons in difficult circumstances.
In the case of Nova Scotia, it receives 2.7 per cent of the total moneys that are distributed under the Canada Assistance Plan and it has a population of 3.5 per cent. Nova Scotia is one of the have-not provinces. Obviously it is unfair that that province should be receiving less than even its per capita share, if Canada Assistance Plan funds were distributed on that basis.
Let us look at British Columbia at the other end of the scale. British Columbia, with 11 per cent of this country's population, receives 14 per cent of the funding from the Canada Assistance Plan.
I will continue with these figures to show the inequity which exists in the distribution but will do so in a somewhat different fashion. I have proposed before and I am proposing again now that the various programs which are handled under the Canada Assistance Plan be divided into their two parts, social service programs and income support programs. I am not suggesting any decrease in funding. In fact, I will be suggesting later that my method of handling these programs would result in some increase in funding at the federal level, but that the distribution of those funds would be more equitable.
Once again in the case of my own province of Quebec, the social service payments are the highest of any province. One would think that in a have-not province the income maintenance programs would be the highest in the province of Quebec, but that is not so. We find other provinces that have a higher income maintenance receipt from the Canada Assistance Plan than the province of Quebec. Quebec's social service receipts are approximately 50 per cent of the amount Quebec receives for the income maintenance programs, whereas New Brunswick, which is one of the have-not provinces, receives for its social service programs only about 15 per cent of the amount it receives in the income maintenance programs. Newfoundland receives about one-quarter and it is about one-third in Nova Scotia. It is interesting that the province of Quebec receives about three times the amount in the social service field that is paid in the province of Ontario.
One notes from a chart provided by the Department of National Health and Welfare, for which the latest figures available are also over a year old, that the province of Nova Scotia, one of the have-not provinces, receives $67 on a per capita basis. The province of Quebec at the other end of the scale receives $137. Dividing the program into its two parts, one can look at social assistance where Manitoba is at $36 at the low end of the scale and Quebec is at $93 at the other end on a per capita basis. With respect to social and welfare services we find New Brunswick sitting on the bottom end of the scale at $14 per capita and Quebec near the top at $44 per capita. It should be abundantly clear that the distribution of
funds under these programs is, in my opinion, an unequitable method of distribution.
For clarification I should say that as a result of changes made in legislation some six or seven years ago, many of the extended health care services which originally were covered under this program have now been excluded. I think it is worth putting on the record that the Canada Assistance Plan no longer covers such items as nursing home intermediate care, adult residential care, converted mental hospitals, home care and ambulatory health care. I mention that because one should consider whether in this day and age those particular services, which are often optional in the provinces, should be funded by the federal government to at least encourage the provincial governments, which are responsible for these services, to provide a relatively equal level of services from coast to coast. 1 wish to quote the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) as follows:
The federal government shares in the cost of provincial and municipal social assistance payments as well as certain social service programs referred to in the act as "welfare services". Social assistance programs must utilize needs testing, must have an appeals system, and not impose residence requirements.
Welfare services include preventive and protective services such as day care, home support, and counselling, as well as services to support independent living such as homemakers, and meals-on-wheels, rehabilitation services, and community development services.
The level of financial assistance provided to individuals and families and the range of welfare services available to Canadians vary considerably from one part of Canada to another, since both are established by the provinces. Payments and services are not uniform.
The federal government has little influence on the design and delivery of those programs, provinces can choose to provide any form of social service which they, the provinces, deem necessary.
I do not believe we would intend, and certainly I am not suggesting, that we take away from the provinces their right to make their own decisions in those areas. However, there has been a significant influence on the need for social welfare services attributed to action on federal programs that are a federal jurisdictional responsibility. These include, for example, changes to the CIS, unemployment insurance and the child tax credit. One can also list family allowances, OAS, spouse's allowances, veterans' pensions, the Canada Pension Plan and the rent subsidy program, all of which are direct federal payments to individuals.
Despite these many programs of direct assistance to individuals, it was made clear that the poorer provinces are finding it increasingly difficult to fund their 50 per cent of expenditures needed to support welfare and social service programs.
I am trying to make clear that in the field of income maintenance, the federal government has a tremendous influence on the costs that the provinces will have to bear. Again I quote the Minister of National Health and Welfare as follows:
The provinces sought a maximum of autonomy and flexibility to develop services in response to their perception of needs and priorities. The responsibility of provincial departments of social services to report to their legislatures will ensure that Canadians are well informed on the levels of expenditures for social services.
July 15, 1982

If I may, because it is extremely relevant here, I will quote from a submission of the ministers of public welfare of the Atlantic provinces. It reads:
The Atlantic provinces are an economically depressed area. A smaller proportion of the population is in the working age groups. This smaller group must support services for the old and young, which tend to be the groups that require high-cost services. The Atlantic provinces experience long periods of high unemployment rates. Persons that are unemployed for long periods tend to be unskilled or uneducated and eventually drop out of the labour force. This results in a smaller employment base and consequently a lower level of income per person in the Atlantic area than elsewhere in Canada. During periods of very high seasonal unemployment large numbers of short-term assistance recipients are added to what is already a high, hard core case load of assistance recipients. The Atlantic provinces have a poor economic base upon which to rely for the financing of heavy welfare burdens.
In conclusion, the federal contribution to the Canada Assistance Plan does not serve a national goal, is inequitable, does not provide for differing provincial priorities, and does not take into account inequality of need or inequality of capacity to provide the revenues to support the provincial share of the program.
I know that this session is now coming to an end and that nothing will happen for some time. I therefore suggest that we take a serious look at the Canada Assistance Plan, as the government has tried on previous occasions, and come up with a different formula for the distribution of the funds. I suggest as a start that we might, on the income maintenance side, increase the federal contribution from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. I say that because, as I already pointed out, the federal government has a tremendous influence on the income maintenance programs via the many federal programs which provide direct funding to individuals. Because the federal government has so little influence at all on the social services that are provided, which I referred to above, which are a smaller part of the total program, the percentage offered by the federal government should gradually be diminished on that side. I would look eventually for a phasing out of the payments that are made for those services and the transfer of those funds to the income maintenance side. The effective result will be an increase in payments to the provinces in need. If the federal government accepts its responsibilities, in the final analysis this will be a much more equitable transfer of funds under the Canada Assistance Plan.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion presented by the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) gives us the opportunity to deal with two very important subjects which are part and parcel of the motion. First and foremost is the access to information that is afforded to Members of Parliament and to all Canadian citizens with respect to government policies and programs. Second is the effect of the Canada Assistance Plan, which is the focal point of the social welfare system in Canada. I want to speak very briefly about the first of those two points, namely, access to information.
When you look at motions such as the one proposed by the hon. member for Vaudreuil, the other motions on the Order Paper as well as the questions listed on the Order Paper, and they number in the thousands, you recognize immediately that
Canada Assistance Plan
the Government of Canada is not willing to provide the kind of information that Members of Parliament seek and other Canadians must have in order properly to assess government policies and programs. The motion today is another example of the need to make information available for the purpose of assessing government policies and programs.
We thought in this House of Commons that we had provided part of a solution to that problem when we passed Bill C-43, the Access to Information and Privacy Act, but days and weeks go by and nothing happens. All I can do is again to repeat the request I made on numerous occasions in the past to have this vital legislation passed by the Parliament of Canada, proclaimed by the governor in council and implemented by the ministry of government responsible for this important measure.
If we had available to us the processes and procedures provided by the Access to Information and Privacy Act, we would not in many cases have to make motions seeking information and place questions on the Order Paper and then wait weeks, months and sometimes years for any sort of answer.
Once again I recognize that the broad solution to the problem of information and the availability of information is general legislation. We now have that kind of legislation. I hope the government will recognize its obligation and immediately act to proclaim and implement this particular legislation.
The second matter raised by the motion is the Canada Assistance Plan and its role in social welfare services. It might be worthwhile to record that the plan is simply a statute of the Parliament of Canada enacted in 1966. It outlines in some detail the nature and extent of the services which can be made available through the provinces and municipalities. The services are much broader than people realize.
Basically, the purpose of all the services, those listed in the Canada Assistance Plan, is to provide necessary assistance to those in need. It does not take much imagination to realize what constitutes a person in need. The services that are provided under the plan consist of basic requirements for food, clothing, shelter, fuel, utilities, household supplies and personal requirements. In addition, services may include the special needs of people, like house alterations and rehabilitation of dwellings. The plan can provide services in health care, specifically those services not covered by the universal health care system.
The importance of these services that can be provided for the aged and the handicapped is underlined by our current economic crisis. I would like to make some remarks about the Canada Assistance Plan and our social services system in Canada in the light of the economic crisis and the measures taken in the budget of June 28. It is evident from that budget that Canada is in deep economic trouble, with a $20 billion deficit facing us and an indication that the deficit may be even higher. This focuses attention on the need for restraint in government spending. The people of Canada, and especially

July 15, 1982
Canada Assistance Plan
Members of Parliament, must recognize the need for a restraint policy. We must be careful that in the course of restraint in government expenditure and services we do not deny the basic needs of the citizens. We must carry out our obligations to them, especially to those who are in dire need of these services.
We must exercise common sense and good judgment. We must realize that there are fates worse than financial difficulty. We must recognize that some elements of service are absolutely basic; they were provided for Canadians in the past and people will continue to depend on them in the future. I want to refer particularly to the requirements of women and of senior citizens. They are most affected by the current economic crisis and the high rate of inflation and the lower value of the Canadian dollar. But before that, we must think of the major problems faced by our almost 2 million unemployed. We know there are 1.3 unemployed and looking for work, and probably another 500,000 who have given up seeking work or are employed at jobs lower than those they are qualified for. We must also think of those employed on a part-time basis. In Canada we have an unemployment insurance system which provides, for a limited period of time, assistance for persons who have been working but have lost their employment. In many cases, unemployed Canadians have gone beyond that point, their unemployment insurance benefit has been exhausted and they are simply without any opportunities to earn the money they need for their subsistence. Consequently, many of those people are thrown on the welfare system. Their only recourse is to apply at the appropriate level of government for welfare assistance.
This unemployment problem has an immediate effect on our social welfare system. It has that effect because of the specific method of dealing with the needs of the unemployed in the unemployment insurance program, the funds of which have been exhausted for many of them.
We know that the additional demand on the unemployment insurance funds has caused an increase in expenditure of some $2 billion, but we do not seem to realize that we can expect a similar increase in expenditures in respect of social assistance. It is difficult to project exactly how many million dollars this will cost government at various levels, but we know the sum will be substantial.
This is an open-ended liability for the provincial and federal governments provided for under the Canada Assistance Plan. The services are based on a right which was granted through legislation to those persons who need these services. There is a mandatory aspect to the provisions. Consequently, once these services are put in place and the eligibility method is determined, the individuals who seek these services have a right to them. As the member for Vaudreuil said, there is a means test employed in order to determine eligibility. Appeals can be made by those persons who believe they have been unfairly denied services. We must realize that, in spite of the economic crisis, the government is under an obligation to provide these services.
At a time when there may be pressure on government to change not only the services available but the restrictions and
the criteria for establishing eligibility, in order to limit the financial drain that arises from the increased demand for these services, there arises a problem which must be solved and that must be faced by the government and by all Canadians. We are in a time of restraint and economic difficulty, even a crisis, but we must recognize the obligations that have been developed in the past and must be continued in the future.
It may seem more sensible to restrict or even withdraw some of the services provided through the Canada Assistance Plan in the past because of our economic difficulties, but if we restrict those services or deny them to those in need, we will create greater problems. If we deny basic food, clothing, shelter and health services to those in need, we will create greater problems. It could lead to the splitting up of families, or to children left unattended or uncared for, and that would have a snowball effect, and that social difficulty would lead to even greater problems. Then we would have to look forward to having to support the kind of persons from whom we withdraw services, in institutions, in hospitals, in prisons, in custodial care institutions. We will not escape the problem by withdrawing services or increasing the requirements for access to those services.
I would like to take the time remaining to underline very briefly the importance of some of the services included in the Canada Assistance Plan and in our social services system. 1 want to direct my remarks particularly to the situation in which many Canadian women find themselves, particularly Canadian women in their senior years. We have come to realize that our pension system in Canada does not properly provide protection for women when they reach their senior years. In our concern for restraining expenditures 1 hope we will not fail to recognize the special plight of senior women in Canada. For younger women, particularly women in the work force who may have to work at relatively menial and low-paying jobs, we must recognize the importance of daycare and assistance for daycare. If we do not provide services like daycare services for the children of working parents, and particularly of single women, then we will simply create a social problem we will have to deal with down the road. There again we cannot neglect our obligations with respect to services like daycare as they apply particularly to working mothers because that will simply produce greater problems in the future.
1 want to deal very briefly with the plight of senior citizens across Canada. Many of our senior citizens find it necessary to utilize the facilities provided in homes for the aged and, in some cases, special care homes like nursing homes. Again, much of the financing for that kind of care has been provided through the Canada Assistance Plan and the provincial legislation which implements the Canada Assistance Plan in the various provinces of Canada. We have to realize and recognize that those kinds of services are absolutely essential, even if we continue in a period of restraint.
I know that on previous occasions the hon. member for Vaudreuil has raised in this House the matter of the need to
July 15, 1982

review the whole basis for our social services and, indeed, the whole basis for other services in the health care field, and part of that review should be reconsideration of the test of universality in the provision of these services.
I want to record my appreciation of the concern of the hon. member for Vaudreuil about the situation in Atlantic Canada. Part of the consideration and review of our social services system should be the implementation of the constitutional provisions with respect to regional disparity. We in this House of Commons have passed legislation respecting the Constitution, which contains a Charter of Rights and Freedoms. That legislative package was approved by the Parliament of the United Kingdom and endorsed very recently in Ottawa by Her Majesty the Queen. The principle of regional disparity is dealt with in those constitutional provisions; no area or region of Canada should suffer a lower standard of living or a lower standard of government services than any other region of Canada. As the hon. member for Vaudreuil graphically pointed out, if we permit the Government of Canada to finance services in one rich part of Canada on the same basis as those services are financed in a poor part of Canada, we will not be implementing the principle of equalization of government and public services across Canada. What I am saying-perhaps too complicatedly-is that what we have to do is re-examine the financing and the method by which the Government of Canada supports social services across the country.
I think it is very important for Canadians to realize that in poorer provinces like Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick government spends a greater amount of its revenue on the provision of necessary social services and health care services than in richer provinces. The governments of those poorer provinces tend to spend a great deal more per capita to provide services because the people in those areas, because of economic difficulties, require more services from government. These are two important factors which ought to be taken into account in a review of our social welfare system in Canada, and I think that review is long overdue and must be undertaken very shortly, if we are to implement, in a real way, the principle of equal services for Canadians right across the country, which we in this House have endorsed.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am sorry that because of the way things have worked out I will not have more time to go into a more extended commentary on some of the things which have been said about the Canada Assistance Plan this afternoon, particularly since the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) and I served on the same task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. If there had been more time, perhaps we could have renewed some of the debates we had about the Canada Assistance Plan at that time.
Basically, I agree with the motion. One of the problems brought to the attention of our task force as we went across Canada was that there are people involved in social service work who cannot seem to find out from their respective provincial governments just what is cost-shared under the
Canada Assistance Plan
Canada Assistance Plan and what is not cost-shared. They get the runaround from their various provincial governments. Any suggestion which would increase the availability of information to people involved in these important services would be a good beginning. Indeed, that is what the task force recommended. It recommended that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) have a Canada Assistance Plan manual compiled to include all guidelines, notes and administrative directives and that this manual be made public, with appropriate provision to respond to questions by the public on its application. It also recommended that the Canada Assistance Plan requirements for statistical and financial information be strengthened to improve understanding of the programs cost-shared under the plan. This need for more information was something recognized by the task force, and I hope it is something the government will look at when it gets around to reviewing the Canada Assistance Plan.
I think there are a great many improvements to the Canada Assistance Plan which need to be made, but one of the anxieties I noted among witnesses at the hearings of the task force was that they had the feeling that whenever the government moves to review something these days, it moves to find out how to save more money and how to spend less money in a particular area rather than how to improve service or how to spend more money. I think there are many people in this country who would just like the government to leave the Canada Assistance Plan alone, with all its warts and all its faults, because we saw what happened when we moved to block funding of health care. We have seen what has happened recently with respect to fiscal arrangements. As much as many people in the country would like the government to review the Canada Assistance Plan in such a way as to help needier provinces and expand the interpretation of what can be cost-shared under the Canada Assistance Plan so that more innovation can take place and new areas of social service can come under the mandate of the Canada Assistance Plan, and as much as those kinds of things are desired by those who are knowledgeable in this field, they are very nervous and worried that the minute the government begins to review the Canada Assistance Plan the first criterion of that review will be how to push more of the fiscal responsibility for these programs onto the provinces and how to get the federal government into such a position that it is paying out less than it now pays under the Canada Assistance Plan.
For all its need for improvement, the Canada Assistance Plan is still one of the few programs left under which there is federal-provincial cost sharing, and in so far as the task force is concerned and many other people involved in this area would like to see a return to some kind of cost sharing in other areas where cost sharing has been abandoned, we find that the Canada Assistance Plan remains an example of how things used to be before we entered into this period of restraint in which, rather than maintaining its commitment to these programs, the federal government is now trying to find its way out of programs under which there has been so much federal-provincial co-operation over the last few decades.

Mr. Speaker, the bill of which debate will be closed on second reading if this closure motion passes, is the primary instrument in the government's fight against inflation. Its provisions are the foundation of the 6 per cent dream world of the last budget. The government is not only restricting debate on the 6 per cent and 5 per cent provisions that affect the wages of federal employees, it is also laying the foundaton of its whole program for the 6 per cent and 5 per cent world.
This evening I believe I am speaking on behalf of all Canadians, whether pensioners, retired federal employees who will be restricted to a 6 per cent increase, or active federal employees who are losing all their rights under this legislation. This bill is flying under false colours, Mr. Speaker. It is supposed to be a bill to control wages of federal employees but it does more than that.
What the government is doing in its attempt to choke off debate on this very important issue, is preventing the public from knowing what the bill actually says. There have been only four days of debate on the bill and of those, last Friday and Wednesday were short days.
Most individuals and groups affected by the bill do not know its provisions. They do not know, if they are active federal employees, that they will be restricted to wage increases of 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next year. They do not know that women employees, who already receive very low wages, will have a larger wage differential as a result of this program. They do not know that those people who earn $9,000-and we
gave some examples in this debate already-or $10,000 or $11,000 or $12,000 per year, will be making the real sacrifice for those who earn $90,000, $100,000, $110,000 or $120,000 a year.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, there are the Jack Horners of this world who will benefit from this bill and there are the cleaning ladies, the nurses' aides, the teachers' aides and the instrument workers who earn $10,000 per year and may be restricted to 6 per cent increases, which will not come close to meeting the increase in the cost of living. These people have not had an opportunity to find out what is in the bill.
By voting tonight we deny the public the opportunity to participate in the debate. We deny the public, whether they be federal employees, pensioners or others concerned with the bill, the opportunity to find out what is in it and to tell their MPs what they think.
The Liberal government agreed to collective agreements with its employees, but now it will not honour them. Ten months ago the government and its ministers who sit opposite, signed agreements with federal employees for 10, 11 and 12 per cent increases-increases less than the cost of living, despite what our Tory friends think. Now the government is saying that despite signed collective agreements those employees will only receive 6 and 5 per cent increases over a two-year period.
That is a direct contradiction of the answer given today by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) when he was asked if the government will also control energy costs which are scheduled to increase by 31 per cent next year. Would the government admit that energy prices should only increase by 6 per cent? No, Mr. Speaker. The minister had the audacity to say in this House that we must honour our agreements. That is the reply from the same government that will not honour the collective agreements which it has signed with its employees. If this debate were allowed to continue, the public would hear about that.
Many of the people who will be affected by this bill do not know about the worst provision it contains. They do not know that it will take away the right of federal employees to negotiate collective agreements with the government. It does not matter whether those agreements include monetary or nonmonetary items. As a result of Bill C-124, employees will not be allowed to negotiate at all. That is the message that is not getting out to the public because there has only been four days' debate on the bill, because the debate is taking place in July and because the media has not covered it very extensively. It means that the people affected by the legislation have not had a chance to make their voices heard.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad to close this debate on behalf of the rabble over here this evening. Mr. Speaker, second reading serves two purposes, and I am delighted to have this opportunity to inform the members of the NDP about those two purposes. The first purpose is to debate the underlying principle of a bill. In the debate we have had on those principles the opponents of this bill have argued that it addresses the wrong issue, that it makes perhaps the most vulnerable part of our society into a scapegoat, and that it has the potential of substantially lowering our standard of living. Those who support the bill argue that there must be restraint at this time for, if there is not, the drop in our standard of living will ultimately be more precipitous and damaging than if no action had been taken. They argue that members of the executive, legislative and judicial branches of the government and the members of the civil service must lead by example and by serving as models of restraint. Those are the basic positions generated in this House. I outline these not because I feel compelled to place these positions of principle before the House, but to tell you that every one of these arguments came out on the very first day of debate.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: And they are equally true today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext:
There has been nothing added to those six basic positions in the four days of debate. So I would argue that the first purpose of second reading has already been accomplished.
The second purpose, Mr. Speaker, is to uncover those issues which are inherent in the bill or to project issues into the bill. From what I have heard in this House and read in Hansard, these are the issues which have been uncovered or projected in this debate. They are: the apparent failure of wage control in the mid 1970s; the deleterious impact on the economy of
Time Allocation
withdrawing funds which otherwise would have been spent on consumer purchases; the apparent suspension of collective bargaining, with its particularly harsh impact on females; the arbitrary separation of the Siamese twins, CN and CP; the uncomfortable position of those bargaining units in the twilight zone; that is, units which, not having signed a contract before budget date, and apparently not being included in the transitional bargaining units, have signed in fact on the very day the budget was brought down; the application of the wage restraints to Crown corporations; the flat, iniquitous approach of the 6-5 solution; and the importance of finding sources of money to spend on job-creation programs without increasing the deficit.
Those are all important issues, Mr. Speaker, and the most important thing about them is that they were all put forward in the first two days of debate. So I would argue that, although there have been subsequent speeches, many of them forceful and some eloquent, but most of them florid, there has not been a single issue uncovered or projected in this debate in the last three days.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: Not true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-124
speechtext: Everyone in this House knows that the real work in Parliament is done in committees. That is where you have the opportunity to bring the general public into the debate, as some hon. members opposite have argued. If the principles have already been delineated in this debate, if the issues have all been raised, if we all know that the only chance the public will have to get involved in this debate is in committee, and we all know that the opportunity for real work on Bill C-124 lies in committee, then why are we abusing the patience and courtesy of this House by prolonging this debate on second reading? Let us go to committee; let us get down to work.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am upset to have to rise in this debate because it is another confrontational debate created by the government party which refuses to pay attention to Parliament, to listen to Members of Parliament or do anything to pay attention to the debate.
