speakeroldname: Mr. Remi Bujold (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when the House rose yesterday afternoon, we were discussing the

July 15, 1982

problems facing thousands of Canadian businesses which forced them to close down because of the present economic situation and lay off thousands of workers. It is clear that the bill now before the House concerning a wage freeze in the public service is meeting with some resistance on the part of employees, but I think that all employees affected by this bill will agree that in the industries I was referring to earlier, we have people who have no job security at all. In situations like the one we are in now, workers are faced with mass lay-offs. In the public service, however, including Crown corporations and all the agencies listed under Schedule II of the bill, employees will agreee that they do have some degree of job security, and what is more, that their particular group does not have to cope with the pressure experienced by employees faced with lay-offs and by their families who have to cope with all kinds of family problems as a result. As I have just said, Mr. Speaker, the employees in the public service and Crown corporations who are affected by Bill C-124 and the wage freeze do not have to face that kind of problem. I think the federal public services, the provincial public services and most of the municipal services are very fortunate in having job security to the extent that they do.
In fact, what we are asking the people affected by this bill is to share with their fellow Canadians some of the benefits they have been able to obtain and acquire during the years they have been employed in the public service. We are also asking them to share these benefits with other fellow citizens who are faced with the extremely difficult situations we are seeing today. We are not asking them to make such sacrifices gladly. We are simply asking them to share with other Canadians what they have been able to obtain, so that at the end of the two-year period imposed by this bill, there will be new confidence in Canada. We want all Canadians to continue to believe in the vast potential of this country and we want people who have their own business to help as many Canadians as possible obtain jobs and earn a decent wage so that they can make a living and raise their families. Mr. Speaker, it seems that the opposition parties agree to some extent with the wage freeze and the temporary wage reduction in the public service. Each and everyone of our friends opposite may have devised various solutions or commented on some provisions of this bill, Mr. Speaker, but all have agreed that the government had to take concrete steps to solve the economic problems facing Canada. Of course, we would have liked to obtain useful ideas and suggestions from our hon. friends opposite during this debate but, as usual, they merely criticized the bill without giving us the co-operation we are seeking from all Canadians at this time. Again today, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and other cabinet ministers responsible for economic matters have met with groups and unions in an attempt to obtain from them the cooperation I referred to earlier. It is clear that if we fail to obtain their co-operation, it will be difficult for us to overcome this economic crisis.
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
If the Prime Minister of Canada, the Minister of Finance, all the Ministers and all members on the government side can meet with people who do not always share their views, why can our friends opposite not do likewise? Why can the Leader of the Opposition not try to convince his friends across the country that we must address the current problems and seek solutions all together? Why can the Leader of the New Democratic Party not try to sit with his trade unionist friends to consider with them the kind of solutions likely to deal with inflation in Canada? That should be the thrust of our action, Mr, Speaker. It is with this purpose in mind that all members of the House, all groups and individuals concerned with the economic situation in Canada, and eager to find solutions to our economic problems, may help the government perform the task it has taken on.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the private sector will also have a major part to play in this endeavour. If the Prime Minister, the cabinet ministers and all the people concerned about the economic situation meet with representatives of all sectors of private enterprise, it is precisely to try to convince them that they should contribute to the solution of the problem. It is important that the private sector should stand by the government to solve this problem. According to recent press reports, especially following the budget and the meetings the government had with business circles, their representatives are willing to co-operate with the government in seeking solutions. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read into the record part of an article published in La Presse which shows the willingness of businessmen to cooperate with the Minister of Finance's efforts to grapple with the economic situation. I quote:
The meeting which Prime Minister Trudeau and several of his ministers had with about 40 businessmen representing major Canadian businesses ended on an optimistic note. The Canadian business community is willing to co-operate with the government to bring the inflation rate down to 6 per cent and accordingly companies will attempt to limit their price increases to this level.
Mr. Speaker, the chairman of the board of Power Corporation, Mr. Paul Desmarais, gave the gist of the meeting in these words for the reporters: "There has been a consensus; the businessmen who were there have given massive support to the government. It was unanimous! We have to fight inflation together, the federal government, the provinces, business and labour! We have to bring the deficit and interest rates down to the lowest possible level!" Mr. Speaker, I believe that such a statement following a meeting with 40 businessmen is selfexplanatory. If we now have in Canada-and I shall give other examples later on, Mr. Speaker-businessmen willing to cooperate with the Canadian government to reduce inflation, everyone will have to do his share.
Mr. Speaker, this article in La Presse speaks of a consensus, but first we must obtain a consensus in this House and this is

July 15, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
what I am asking of my friends opposite. Why would they not give this government the consensus which business, unions, workers and organized labour throughout the country are willing to give? Why is it that our friends opposite are not able to do their part, disregard political partisanship and the few votes they could gain in some constituency somewhere in Canada and give us this consensus so that we may use the next two years to get out of the current economic mess? Mr. Speaker, they readily admit that we must fight inflation and attempt everything to solve our present economic problems, but 1 wonder why they do not want to give this consensus to the government. Businessmen and unions are willing to do their share. I am certain that our friends on the extreme left are not very happy to hear that the President of the Canadian Labour Congress came out of a meeting with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) saying he was confident we would find solutions.
Obviously our friends do not really like the president-I was going to say the president of their party-making such statements. However, in view of the present situation, this man was able to sit down and tell the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance: "It is true that we have problems, but I shall put aside some of my opinions, which may be political or labour oriented, to see whether we can resolve these economic problems together." We have been asking for co-operation since the budget speech. We now ask our friends opposite to co-operate and do not understand their reluctance. While many of their constituents have given this kind of co-operation to the government, why will they not for once, Mr. Speaker, forget their political partisanship? Then this House of Commons and the other place can say that henceforth we shall try to work ourselves out of this economic situation within the next two years so that each Canadian, in each constituency, in each region, in each province, can enjoy his share of the wealth of this country.
Comments throughout the world make it abundantly clear that Canada is a country of plenty that inspires envy. We should all think about this and consider that, for once, we are given the opportunity to unite and co-operate so that Canada may continue to be one of those countries which every head of state wants to take as a model and say: "This is a country whose people, heedless of their own personal and political interests, try to find together a way out of an extremely difficult economic situation which affects the entire world." This is the only thing, Mr. Speaker, we are asking of our friends opposite and the Canadian people. Of course we realize we may be blamed for selecting a group of individuals who are readily identifiable and, as I pointed out earlier, who enjoy some privileges over other Canadians. Employees of the Civil Service and Crown corporations indisputably enjoy advantages and privileges other Canadian workers do not have.
Mr. Speaker, you surely have had the experience in your own constituency office, along with the majority of members, of a 45 or 50 year-old man calling on you because his company has recently closed down. He has come to ask you for a job in a related field of employment and tells you that he had been working with the same employer for 25 or 30 years and never expected his company would close down. He tells you that he has two or three school-age children and can't get a job. Each and all of us have dealt with such cases, but this government has taken steps to put an end to such a situation throughout the country.
We have taken measures to help those people. I may have the opportunity to describe a few programs later on. What I wish to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, since your constituency is made up of public servants, is that I would be quite surprised if you told me that you had received the visits of public servants complaining they had lost their jobs because their company had closed down. I do not think there is any prospect of the federal, provincial or municipal governments doing that. Job security is a great advantage government workers have over the others. This is why, Mr. Speaker, we are seeking their co-operation, so that other Canadians who do not enjoy such job security may get secure employment also. We have taken steps, developed programs and implemented plans in Canada to meet those expectations. Allow me to point out that we have just passed new legislation on occupational training at a cost of $1 billion this year to cope with layoffs throughout the country affecting workers of all ages as a result of technological changes in some industries.
These training programs will enable thousands of workers to acquire new skills in certain fields to meet the challenge of today's technology and to work for other companies in different sectors. Perhaps some of my friends opposite think that we are dreaming, but they ought to face reality and see that courses are now being given throughout the country to retrain workers and enable them to gain experience in new technology so they will get jobs in new fields and in industries which have changed considerably in recent years. Mr. Speaker, those are the various areas where our government has invested considerable amounts of money to retrain the labour force.
Naturally, we do not believe that our new budget and the new programs which have been announced will produce instantaneous results and that they will have concrete repercussions throughout the country tomorrow, the day after or perhaps even next week or in the next few months. Our aim is to take steps right away so that in the coming months and especially in the coming year all Canadians everywhere in Canada will respond and co-operate as we expect them to do, because our objective is to develop the whole Canadian economy so that within a few years it will reach what we believe to be its full productive capacity.
July 15, 1982

Of course, Mr. Speaker, some of our friends say that we always blame other countries, but we do have to keep in mind the international economic situation. My friends opposite and all Canadians who believe that the new budget or the new programs to be launched will enable Canada to solve the economic problems of the world have another think coming. We live in a very prosperous country where natural resources are plentiful, but there is no way that 24 or 25 million Canadians can possibly come up with a solution to the economic problems of the United States, Japan, Italy and West Germany. One of my friends said a moment ago that we are dreaming in colour. Mr. Speaker, they are the ones who are dreaming in colour when they ask the government to find a solution to all the problems of the world.
Naturally, a good many people think that we are taking drastic measures, but we have to, Mr. Speaker. First of all, we must show the Canadian people that they have a responsible government that is prepared to do its utmost over the next two years to restore confidence and the economic climate we had before from coast to coast. It would be utopian to think that within our own country we can take measures that will solve the problems of all other countries. Those who think that, be they in the opposition or ordinary Canadians, are dreaming in colour. We will start off by doing whatever is required within Canada to restore that climate of confidence and help the Canadian people.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to touch on another aspect of Bill C-124 which in the next two years will enable the government to recoup some funds by limiting salary increases to 6 and 5 per cent, and then reinvest that money in the regions of the country that need it most. Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to speak of my own region, eastern Quebec, the Gaspe Peninsula, and in particular of the riding of Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine. It may be that our honourable friends opposite and a few other members of this House are not aware of the fact that in the Gaspe Peninsula and the riding of Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine, the rate of unemployment now ranges from 50 to 60 per cent. The people in those areas are Canadians like all the others, Mr. Speaker, they are entitled to the same rights, privileges and opportunities as all other Canadians. There lies the responsibility of the government, Mr. Speaker: it must see to it that funds are garnered in other sectors of activity and reallocated with a view to helping the people in underdeveloped areas who also want to share in the wealth of this country. Indeed, with the funds that are reallocated and reinvested in direct job creation, we can, through community development projects, give jobs to those people who, in many cases, some time this summer or in early fall, will have exhausted their entitlement to unemployment benefits without having had over that period, because of the current economic situation, the opportunity of going back to the seasonal jobs they had in previous years. Those are the people we will help, Mr. Speaker, by allowing them to work for
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
periods of 20 to 40 weeks and so to provide for their wives and children as other Canadians do across the country.
Those then are the decisions this government had to take, Mr. Speaker. And we took them because our party has always strived to ensure that all Canadians, throughout the land, wherever they live and whatever they do, have the same opportunities, the same advantages. Mr. Speaker, obviously, through Bill C-124 and the measures proposed by the budget, we are asking the majority of Canadians, some sectors of the Canadian population, to make sacrifices. But we must, through this bill and the other measures, convince ourselves that we can, if we are to come out of these difficult times, first of all, as the government-and this, I think we have proved-be assured that we can do so. Above all, Mr. Speaker, I feel that every hon. member, every Canadian, must first convince himself that we are able, that we have the necessary means, that we have the ability, that we have the natural resources and wealth throughout the country to come out of this economic crisis.
Mr. Speaker, it is difficult for an individual to try to convince his fellow citizens or friends if he is not convinced himself that we have the means to do so. That is the attitude, the way of thinking that each and every Canadian must cultivate within himself. With all we have in this country, with our tremendous wealth in natural resources, we can pull out of this economic impasse. That is the only way, Mr. Speaker, for every Canadian, every group, every association, every labour union, every businessman, to convince those around them that we can, that we will achieve that economic renewal we are all seeking and will achieve by the end of those two years, provided every individual does his part. That is what we are asking: first, that everyone do his part in overcoming the current economic situation, and second, that everyone convince himself that we can do so, Mr. Speaker!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
The important one is here now, Mr. Speaker.
Canada is in trouble, big trouble. We have a desperate need for a solution to aid those suffering from unemployment and all Canadians who are subject to all-time high inflation rates. We need action and we need it fast. The social conscience of our nation demands it.

July 15, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
Our unemployment rate is comparable to the rates during the Great Depression when unemployment ranged from 11 per cent to 20 per cent. The unemployment rate of our public sector now effectively stands at 15 per cent. These figures are terrifying and unacceptable to every thinking Canadian. Coupled with unemployment is inflation which is running at an annual rate in excess of 11 per cent. We have record bankruptcies and small business failures, and a lack of confidence in our dollar which really reflects the lack of confidence in Canada as a nation. That hurts, Mr. Speaker, because we know what wonderful, abundant resources this country has; resources in the land as well as its people.
Why, you may ask, why has this happened? How can a country like ours end up in such a mess? I will tell you why. As the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) put it, there has been an alarming drop in commercial investment and profits. The demand for goods has diminished both here in Canada and in our foreign markets. One quarter of our production capacity remains idle. Over the past few years, our industrial productivity has been rising at the second slowest rate of any major industrialized nation. Borrowing costs in Canada are higher than those in most other industrialized nations. What a sorry state for such a rich country!
To come to Canada's rescue, the jaded knights in shining armour, although sadly tarnished at this point, have devised a plan for the economic recovery of the nation. First there was a budget-the third one-born of desperation rather than inspiration. Shameful is the only word to describe the unjust treatment of the old age pensioners who subsist near the poverty line. They are restricted to the same 6 per cent cost of living increase as the presidents of our renowned Crown corporations. These people are the Canadians who created a better way of life for us than they enjoyed, and in more difficult times than these. This is the way the Liberal government thanks them.
1 think all Canadians would prefer that we treat our fathers and mothers and the fathers and the mothers of all members of our generation with compassion and respect and eliminate this disgraceful provision. Then there is Bill C-124, the public sector compensation restraint act, as it is called, created to curb the wage increases of public servants in an attempt to quell inflation.
Mr. Speaker, restraint is an admirable goal when practised in the right direction. But are we really talking about the same thing? It seems to me that the government has a slightly different interpretation of the term "restraint". Its record makes its dedication subject to proof. The government, in its November budget, aimed to curb its spending at 22 per cent. However, only seven months later, its spending did not reduce but, instead, increased by 20 per cent. Is that the example the Canadian people are expected to follow?
The government should show leadership, but it certainly has not to date. Bill C-124 shows inequitable treatment of those categorized as public servants. Lower ranks in the military, for example, paid at very low levels, are asked to risk their lives in crisis times, to move their families and themselves on short
notice, to pay increasing accommodation and utility costs and to use outdated equipment and bear the burden of understaffed personnel. They are being restricted to the same 6 per cent income increase as top military brass, cabinet ministers and generals and admirals. We should not penalize the lower ranks further.
The potential for creating union problems is manifest in the provisions regarding transportation unions which have traditionally bargained in the same sector. Provisions which make restraint measures applicable against the CNR are not similarly applicable against the CPR. Measures which cap the wages of Air Canada employees do not similarly cap the wages of employees of Canadian Pacific Air, Eastern Provincial Airways, or other regional carriers. It is to be hoped that these measures would in effect apply with equal fairness to all persons within the transportation sector.
Such equity is not envisioned by these measures. While I can support the principle of restraint, I look forward to correcting these inequities in committee so that I, and indeed all Canadians, can support the substance of the bill when it is before us.
I would prefer that the government place before Parliament a comprehensive program to reduce expenditures by supplying government services to all Canadians at the lowest possible cost. It should invest in committees the right to make accountable all those who in the past and in the future by their decisions have or can cost Canadians millions of dollars in waste, extravagance and mismanagement. Cuts or delays in discretionary spending in most departments are imperative. To lead the economic recovery of our nation I recommend the elimination of the capital gains tax and major changes in FIRA in order to attract badly needed capital investment. I feel the use of our resources and the advantages to Canadians can be controlled without discouraging investment in the manner now being done. I suggest the revenue from the capital gains tax is small compared with the benefits which will accrue through taxation of income generated by investment. I recommend that major tax incentives be provided for industrial research and development which can give Canadian industry a badly needed edge in competition for world markets essential to the economic recovery and development of our nation.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, more flexible caps on indexing, ranging from full indexation for low-income people to none for fat cats earning $50,000 and over, including the top brass such as ministers, deputy ministers and Members of Parliament is, in my view, a more equitable and fair method of leading the war on inflation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just forget who said it, but there is a saying that those who do not learn from history are condemned to repeat it. That is what is happening today, and that is what happened in 1975. There is another quotation I would like to give you, and I hope some hon. gentlemen from the government side or the official opposition can identify the person who said it. It was to the
July 15, 1982

effect that labour is prior to and superior to capital, and without labour, capital cannot function. I am not sure that any of my colleagues in the other two parties can identify who said that, so for their edification let me tell them that it was said by Abraham Lincoln in 1856. If you have $1 million of capital and no one will work for you, your capital is worth nothing.
The principle of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is wrong. The bill itself is wrong. If you limit through legislation the pay and allowances of one group, if you limit their rights, if you can do it to that one group, then of course the door is wide open to do it to any other group. One would think in these times that the government and this Parliament would bring in legislation which challenges the entire nation, which makes us all equal in this battle, this national economic emergency, and which will bring us out of an economic depression. It is a depression, so let us not delude ourselves with a milder word like "recession". I said that those who do not learn from history are condemned to repeat it, and one only has to look at Hansard between 1928 and 1938 to see the truth of that. Let me give some quotes, such as the following:
During the summer, coming events began to cast their shadow over international finance ... The proposals of President Hoover for a one-year moratorium were heralded as a signal for returning world confidence, but the optimism was unfortunately short lived .. . Well may Canadians look back with satisfaction over what has been accomplished.
That was a fellow by the name of E. N. Rhodes, Minister of Finance, April 6, 1932, as reported at pages 1749 and 1750 of Hansard. He was a Conservative. Let us go to another one. This one was a tirade, and it reads as follows:
There were increases in the public debt, bringing the public debt to a point higher than it has reached at any previous time in Canada ... Where we might have hoped for some evidence of decreases in the general cost of government, there has been but little.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have endeavoured to make it appear that this condition has been due to world conditions.
That was the right hon. leader of the Liberal official opposition, one William Lyon Mackenzie King, April 26, 1932, as reported at pages 2363 and 2364 of Hansard.
Let us go to another one, which reads:
The evidence of business recovery is written incontrovertibly in the recorded facts of our industry and trade.
That is again the Minister of Finance, Mr. Rhodes, as reported on April 18, 1934, at page 2267 of Hansard.
Let us move now to another regime because I am endeavouring to show they are, both of them, still the same old bunch. Here is another quote:
With respect to the income tax, charged as we were with increasing it, the minister was frank the other evening in saying that he had increased it slightly. And so all along the line we have the same position.
That is one R. B. Bennett, March 2, 1937, as reported at page 1391 of Hansard. Mr. Speaker, the then leader of the opposition, following his government from 1930 to 1935, moved an amendment to the Liberal budget which said:
This House regrets that the government has failed to take effective measures to deal with the problem of unemployment.
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
What we are getting today? The Herbert Hoover's, the R. B. Bennett's and the Mackenzie King's are now telling us again-they have not learned from history-to tighten our belts, show restraint and pick out some people who are easy victims, easy to pick on. The fellows who said in the dirty thirties that prosperity is just around the corner are telling us the same thing again. All you have to do is to slap on a 6 per cent limit for public servants and Crown corporation employees, and then somehow or other that will automatically result in everyone else in the economy rushing to volunteer to restrict increases in their incomes to not more than 6 per cent.
I have not heard any mad stampede or scramble outside the doors of this chamber, or anywhere else in this country, to volunteer, but the ones who do not learn from history and are now repeating it say things like:
Yes, I would continue to back Mr. Bouey. I agree that our interest rates have to track those in the United states.
That was said by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). Imagine that.
Here is another quote which reads:
We have looked for a solution other than the government's, but we couldn't come up with an alternative ... At this moment, I don't have a better solution.
I presume he meant, other than horizontal with the Liberals. That was the right hon. gentleman from Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) as reported in the Toronto Star on May 5.
By the way, the quotation I read from the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) is from a CTV interview on June 7, 1981. The Liberals had not even been in office all that long, and he was already telling us how great Governor Bouey and the Liberals were doing.
We must consider the whole matter of honesty and integrity in federal politics. 1 have another quote which reads:
-our leaders have got to be a little less honest . . . we're not being devious and tricky enough ... I'm criticizing us for that.
That was the hon. gentleman from St. John's West from the "Watson Report" of February 4, 1979.
The same gentleman is reported in Maclean s magazine for July 12, 1981 as saying the government:
-is adrift; it has no answers. If I told you what I would do, we'd never get elected.
The hon. member for St. John's West said that, I did not.
With respect to controls and wages, here is another quote:
What is in the budget? There is one important initiative ... the introduction of restraint on public sector salaries. That is a field in which the government has lagged behind several Canadian provinces. All of which, by the way, during times when we had Tory governments.
This quote continues:
We are relieved that it is beginning to accept that government spending is a major cause of current economic problems ... it is a step in the right direction.
Those words are from the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition pertaining to the restraint measures on the public servants and the Crown corporation employees in Canada.

July 15, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
Neither one of the parties have learned anything. Neither one of them have the courage to adopt something different from and more than what they tried before.
I am just an innocent prairie boy and I always understood that if you charged people more, it will cost you more. I did not think there was anything complicated about that. If you have higher interest rates, that means the cost of everything goes up. I thought, even when I was in public school, that was automatic. You pay higher prices for everything you buy. You pay higher mortgages. You have higher unemployment. You pay higher costs of production if you are a producer, and generally you have higher costs of living if you raise and keep raising or keep interest rates high. The evidence is in. The jury does not even have to meet. The high interest rate policy has meant higher unemployment, a higher cost of living, bankruptcies and the whole litany.
Why does the Liberal government and the Conservative opposition still clutch on to something that went out of date in the dirty thirties? It did not work then. It is not working now, and it will not work now.
A number of my colleagues have talked about the freedoms that are denied in this bill. I was in this chamber when we voted on the War Measures Act. Those of us who said it should not happen, and those of us who were ruled out by closure were subsequently vindicated by the right hon. gentleman, the former member for Halifax and the former leader of the Progressive Conservative Party-and if the Tories had had any brains they would have kept him and he would be prime minister right now-who said a few years later that he wished he had done what Tommy Douglas did; he wished that he had voted against the implementation of the War Measures Act. It may be in the makeup of the person who is the leader of the official opposition to say down the road a few months or a few years that he wished he had voted against this bill because it denies the integrity of a bargaining unit.
This bill does away with protection from sexual harassment. It does away with negotiating for parental leave, it does away with pensions for part-time workers, vacation leave, paid holidays, pre-retirement leave, job classifications, job security, technological changes, contracting out, dental and health plans, improved bereavement leave and grievance procedures. All of those things are done away with. This is a new War Measures Act. This is not the kind of length a Parliament or any political party has to go to in order to bring about an alleviation of what we all know to be an economic national emergency, an economic depression. It is plain for everyone to know, to experience and to see.
We suggest there is a different way. I cannot say we are 100 per cent certain that it will work 100 per cent. But I can say that it is something different, something more than and different from what has been the conventional wisdom. I want to suggest that in order to deal with this matter, in order to get the co-operation, in fact, the enthusiastic support of our fellow citizens, we have to bring in measures that are not only fair but are seen to be fair. The perception out there in our riding is that all of us in this war should stop the depression and start
an expansion of our economy and that everyone should be treated fairly and equitably. I do not believe and I do not think anyone else does that this legislation is going to result automatically in fellow Canadians saying, "Well, they have limited the public servants and the Crown corporation employees to 6 per cent next year and 5 per cent the year after." And as a result of that, they are all going to volunteer and take the pledge to limit their increases.
I have talked to my lawyer, my doctor, my chartered accountant and my real estate buddies, and none of them have volunteered to follow suit. In fact, they are laughing. I have not heard of Mr. Bronfman volunteering to fall in line with what is happening to public servants. He only received $1,064,288 last year. I have not heard him volunteering to take only a 6 per cent increase next year and 5 per cent the year after. I do not know why he would not, because 6 per cent would mean another $63,800; then he would be living up to the spirit of this legislation. Then there is J. A. de Grandpre from the mother Bell outfit. Last year the poor fellow only made $626,000. Not even he has rushed forward to volunteer to follow the example which was arbitrarily laid upon public servants and employees of Crown corporations by limiting his increase to 6 per cent, which would amount to a paltry $37,500. I do not see him rushing forward.
Let me turn to the area of Crown corporations. Well, by law CNR employees will receive 6 per cent next year and 5 per cent the year after. Dr. LeClair, the new president of the Crown corporation, only received something in the order of $240,000 last year.
An hon. Member; It was $200,000.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Perhaps it was only $200,000. Eventually we will find out from the interstate commerce commission of the United States, but let us assume that it was only $200,000. The poor fellow will have to volunteer to take an increase of only $12,000 next year, which is what janitors and other low-paid workers in the public service receive in the way of entire incomes. I fully expect a grand announcement in another week or two that Dr. LeClair has agreed to a freeze in his salary. He was only obtaining $200,000, but who would not agree to a freeze on $200,000 which will amount to another $12,000.
This is not the way to attack inflation or to solve a national economic emergency. We should not do what was done in the dirty thirties nor what was tried in 1975; it did not work. I listened to a previous speaker talking about putting people to work. This was done by R. B. Bennett and Mackenzie King. 1 saw the relief camps of the dirty thirties-two bits a day and your grub. Their solution is to attack the victims, not the perpetrators. The first people they pick on are the first victims of inflation and the first victims of economic depression-wage earners, pensioners and low-income people. The Liberals, supported by the Tories, as was the case in the dirty thirties, attack these people.
July 15, 1982

If they want to set an example for all Canadians to follow, they should start at the top and work down. They should say to the corporate elite, to financial institutions and to high income people, including Members of Parliament, that they will lead the way. To leave out those who in fact are the causes of economic depression is the worst kind of injustice.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the former minister of finance both think that Gerald Bouey is the best thing since sliced bread. Both of them have said that his policy on interest rates is also their policy. They are fundamentally wrong. In order to get out of this economic depression, this national emergency, square one is interest rates. We say that the government must instruct the Bank of Canada to reduce interest rates tomorrow to the level of inflation or not more than one per cent above it. If that means selective foreign exchange controls or total foreign exchange controls, so be it, for the length of the national economic emergency.
Whether someone wants to send $300,000 or $3 million out of the country, we would not allow it. But the ones who want to send hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country to invest in what can be nothing more than greed, selfishness, and traitorous behaviour, in order to make fast bucks out of shopping centres, luxury apartments or real estate in the United States, should be told that they cannot do so. If this country is big enough to make a profit out of, it is good enough to invest in. For a change, the people with investment capital, whether it is a lowly widow, a millionaire, a bank or a trust company, should be called upon to invest in the nation. If they do not, they should be made to do so. They should be given two choices-it is either compulsory or they have to.
This is the case in western European countries and Japan. They not only have planned economies, but in effect they have controlled economies; they always have had. Countries with inflation rates of 7 per cent or 9 per cent or interest rates of 7 per cent or 9 per cent have controlled economies. They have investment policies which collect public and private investment capital to be directed into what are the priorities of the nations.
Surely the priorities are here into which we could direct investment, and investors could obtain a reasonable return on their investment. Let us start with housing. We should not horse around with $500,000. Let us make it $1 billion per year for the next ten years. Then let us turn to transportation and invest in it $1 billion per year for the next 15 years. In fact, $1 billion per year for all modes of transportation would not be enough, but it would be the minimum and it could be public and private investment capital.

subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS-FUTURE OF DALY BUILDING IN OTTAWA
PUBLIC WORKS-FUTURE OF DALY BUILDING IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, following a report in the media, I put a question to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) concerning the demolition of a building in my riding, the Daly Building. Yesterday morning a newspaper in the national capital reported that Treasury Board would have approved the demolition of that building. That report caused quite a stir in my riding, and in Ottawa as well, because some time ago the City of Ottawa has designated that structure as a Heritage building.
The Daly Building, Mr. Speaker, is a federal property that comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works and not under the jurisdiction of the President of the Treasury Board. This is why I directed my question to the Minister of Public Works, because we know he is responsible for the management of federal buildings. This point has to be clarified, because if the minister applied to Treasury Board, it was probably for some supplementary estimates not earmarked in the budget of his department for that building.
In reply to my question, the minister indicated that he would appeal the decision of Treasury Board and that he intended to put the issue in the context of a study now under preparation of the total accommodation within the Ottawa capital region. Since this is a very controversial issue, I would like to provide a brief history of that matter which has been under consideration for at least seven or eight years. The Daly Building is strategically situated in the centre of the national capital within walking distance of Parliament Hill. This prestigious location offers exceptional view and access. The building is located on the corner of Rideau Street and Sussex Drive, next to the Rideau Centre project, now under construction, as everyone knows, and which brings about $200 million in economic activity to the National Capital. The seven storey Daly Building, which was built at the turn of the century, has a total area of 18,600 square meters; it stands on a lot measuring 4,332 square meters. Designed and built in 1905 as a large department store, the Daly Building was converted in 1919 into federal government offices and was to be demolished in 1979 with several obsolescent government buildings, namely the so-called temporary buildings on Sussex Street which were indeed demolished at the time. The building was purchased in 1921 by the federal government and in turn accommodated various departments. However, since the early seventies, the building has become increasingly outdated which has meant

July 15, 1982
Adjournment Debate
that major repairs have had to be made. In 1974, a first study was made to assess the situation and determine whether there would be any point in renovating the building or whether it would be more appropriate to tear it down. In the meantime, consultations were undertaken with various groups in the private and public sectors, which could have been interested in acquiring the building. It was thus offered to various government levels, provincial and municipal, and private interests, including a co-operative, a group of private interests, Crown corporations and many others, but always without success. In fact-and this is quite amusing, Mr. Speaker-in 1978, the Ottawa municipal council even decided that the building should be demolished.
We know the building has been vacant ever since. For the last three years at least, no one has occupied the building except the rats. However, this does not mean that it is not costing anything since it must still be heated and maintained to prevent complete deterioration in case a decision should be made to preserve it. In my opinion, our decision must be based strictly on economic considerations. If renovation is economically justified, the building should be renovated. However, if renovation costs exceed the cost of a new building, it should obviously be demolished. With this in mind, in 1978 I got in touch with the then Minister of Public Works, Mr. Buchanan, to get an idea of the costs. The minister then indicated in a letter that the study on the feasibility of renovation made in 1974 showed that it would cost over $10 million, $10.3 million to be exact for the building to comply with safety standards. At the time, it was estimated that it would cost approximately $250,000 to tear it down. In view of these facts, the decision to demolish the building was made in April 1979 for several reasons which would be too long to explain now. This was not done and we are now facing the same situation as in 1979, namely a controversy. I do not have the exact figures here, Mr. Speaker, but we can assume that since it would have cost over $10 million to renovate the building in 1978, it would certainly cost between $18 million and $20 million in 1982. As for the cost of demolition, it can be estimated at nearly $400,000. Moreover, according to the 1974 study to which I referred earlier and which had to do with the amortization of renovation costs over a 25-year period, it would have been necessary to raise the rent by as much as 50 per cent over that of a new building. One can reasonably assume that the situation has not changed in 1982 and that the same figures apply, although they may have to be readjusted because of inflation.
Yesterday, the minister told me that he would reconsider the situation. I think, therefore, that we would be well advised to wait for these new findings, in order to understand better the costs involved. That is the reason why I support the Minister in his appeal of the decision of Treasury Board and I will wait for the results of the study of the total accommodation of the federal government within the National Capital Region, study which should be completed by this Fall.

speakeroldname: Mr. Henri Tousignant (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS-FUTURE OF DALY BUILDING IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as parliamentary secretary, I am very pleased to be able to answer my hon. colleague and to confirm what he just said, namely that, yesterday, the minister did indeed say that he would appeal a decision made recently by Treasury Board concerning the demolition of the Daly Building, and that he also was considering the feasibility of using the building for the benefit of the National Capital Region. The federal government has been using the Daly Building since 1918, and I would like to take this opportunity to confirm that, since then, the building was occupied without interruption by various federal departments until 1980 when the last federal tenants left the premises.
In 1977, the building was declared surplus to federal needs, because it no longer met present office standards. Since then, Mr. Speaker, the issue has been a very controversial one and has given rise to some very heated debate. In March 1981, Public Works Canada called for proposals from renovators with a view to using the Daly Building again. After due consideration, the Treasury Board ministers reached a decision regarding the future use of the building. As I said before, the Minister of Public Works is prepared to ask his colleagues to review their decision as you requested, in the light of an overall plan for accommodation in the National Capital Region. Furthermore, he intends to make a thorough study of the cost involved in using the building to accommodate federal offices. In this analysis, full consideration will be given to trends in the office building situation in Ottawa and to effective utilization of government resources.
In concluding, I wish to thank the member for Ottawa-Vanier who raised this question in the House. His abiding interest and continued efforts to improve the downtown area of the National Capital are well known. The Daly Building, and especially the building's prestigious location near the Parliament buildings, demands a serious planning approach. For many years, the member for Ottawa-Vanier has put forward excellent arguments in support of sound urban planning in the National Capital downtown area.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-FUNDING FOR SERVICES. (B) CANADIAN MENTAL HEALTH ASSOCIATION MEETING
SOCIAL SECURITY-FUNDING FOR SERVICES. (B) CANADIAN MENTAL HEALTH ASSOCIATION MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to again bring to the attention of the government the fact that bad economic policy produces unemployment and bad economic policy produces stress for human beings. I would remind members of this Chamber that in December 1979 this House rejected a budget that would have created jobs, that would have reduced inflation, that would have produced more help for the poorest segment of our society. Instead, we have
July 15, 1982

bad economic policy, increased unemployment and a financial crisis in many homes.
It is well known that social science literature is full of facts which indicate that when you create unemployment in society you create stress for people. That stress shows up in increased debt, in increased mental health breakdowns, in increased heart attacks, in increased alcoholism, in increased wife beating, and in increased child beating.
If we project on the basis of some of the best scientific literature, when we consider the 3 per cent increase in unemployment which has occurred in the last year, do you know what we are looking at in the year ahead? We are looking at something in the order of a 12 per cent increase in suicides, a 15 per cent increase in homicides, a 12 per cent increase in prison admissions and a 10 per cent increase in hospital admissions. Those people will be the social victims of our bad economic policy.
I have tried to bring those statistics to the attention of this government on more than one occasion, Mr. Speaker. The last time I had an opportunity, on June 14, I brought them to the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) during question period. Prior to that, statistics of this same kind were rejected by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) and by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), who comes from Windsor, Ontario, where there is evidence of those statistics right on the street. If he got out and visited the people in the riding he represents and talked to them, he would find those kinds of social consequences. That is all he would have to do.
The Minister of Labour yelled out that this was not true. I would like to bring to the attention of the House just three studies; the first being a Statistics Canada paper called "Health and Economic Activity" written by O. B. Adams. That kind of information is contained in that study.
Another study was conducted for the Minister of Labour. It is referred to in popular literature as the Carruthers Report. That kind of statistic is given there. Another one was conducted by the Canadian Council on Social Development. Its report was sent to every Member of Parliament in November 1980.
It is incredible to have to stand here, for the fourth of fifth time, to try to bring to the attention of this government the fact that there are social consequences. There is increased debt, increased homicide, increased suicide, increased alcoholism, increased wife and child beating, which is predictable from bad economic policy. People who are losing their jobs, who are losing their homes, are put under stress. Sometimes that stress is unbearable and these consequences flow from it.
I tried to bring these statistics to the attention of the Prime Minister on June 14. I said: "Mr. Prime Minister, when I see this new, marvellous budget, will there be increased funding for the social service sector, for hospitals, for prisons and for treatment facilities?" The Prime Minister said: "Watch, wait and see. Be patient."
Adjournment Debate
We now have the budget, and the tragedy is that there is no increased funding for hospitals; there is no increased funding for prisons; there is no increased funding for social services. The government is creating victims but is not meeting its obligation to go even a little way toward helping those victims. That is a tragedy for the country and for the victims.
The only significant cut this government has made in its exorbitant spending up to this point is a cut out in transfer payments to the provinces. The provinces deliver these social services, yet each day we are seeing in our newspapers increased evidence that the money is not adequate to help the victims of the policy of this government.
I hope the parliamentary secretary will stand up tonight and make a commitment to increased funding for these groups.

speakeroldname: Mr. Henri Tousignant (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-FUNDING FOR SERVICES. (B) CANADIAN MENTAL HEALTH ASSOCIATION MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, federal contributions to the provinces for health care are made under the established programs financing arrangements. Under these arrangements the federal government will contribute some $8.5 billion in 1982-83 in respect of three health-related programs: hospital insurance, medicare and extended health care. The formula on which these contributions is based contains an escalator which is derived from a three-year moving average of nominal gross national product. This escalator was chosen to ensure year-to-year stability of the growth of federal contributions.
As far as social services are concerned, the federal government is continuing to pick up 50 per cent of the provinces' cost under the Canada Assistance Plan. The program is open-ended and supports services to persons in need or likely to become in need. Because federal contributions &d4069;-l are tied to provincial expenditures on the basis of a cost-sharing formula, federal payments rise automatically in line with provincial spending.
In terms of the hon. member's second question concerning the Canadian Mental Health Association meeting, it should be noted that although the Department of National Health and Welfare undertakes a number of joint activities with the CMHA, Department of National Health and Welfare officials were given no notice of the meeting to which the hon. member refers. The mental health division of the Department of National Health and Welfare contacted the CMHA and was informed that this meeting is a private meeting of an internal committee of the CMHA and is viewed by CMHA as a preliminary step toward defining the problem areas and identifying possible or desirable action.
It is perhaps worth noting that the Department of National Health and Welfare, primarily through its mental health division, has had a long-standing relationship with CMHA. In addition to the department's sustaining grant of $39,000 for head office administration, several joint projects have been undertaken between CMHA and the mental health division. These were supported by departmental funding. Examples of these are the production of parent education pamphlets, each advising parents on one particular behavioural problem in childhood and a national symposium on perspectives on the

care of the longer-term mentally ill held in February, 1982. The proceedings of this latter symposium are expected to form the basis of a more detailed report on the care of the chronically psychiatrically ill in Canada. Finally, a CMHA proposal to promote and maintain mental health in the workplace is currently under review within the health promotion directorate of this branch.
In summary, excellent working relationships exist between Health and Welfare Canada and the Canadian Mental Health Association. Officers of the mental health division serve on a number of CMHA committees, though not on the committee to which the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) has apparently referred.
Regarding the specific meeting in question, the department would be glad to receive any suggestions for possible action on preventive strategies to reduce mental health service demands, consequent to employment loss.

MEDICAL CARE-EXTRA BILLING BY PHYSICIANS-MINISTER'S POSITION. (B) FEDERAL FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 11 I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) a question about extra billing by doctors. At that time I was after the minister for agreeing with provincial health ministers to control extra billing rather than eliminating it, a position which in my view meant she was backing down from her previous views on extra billing.
On July 14 I asked the minister what she intended to do about lay-offs in health care services in Nova Scotia and the introduction of user fees in the hospitals of that province.
On both those occasions I tried to make the point that the Minister of National Health and Welfare seriously damaged her bargaining power with the provinces when she allowed the reduction in treasury transfer payments to the provinces proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), and which took effect when the established programs financing arrangements were pushed through in the spring of this year. I said then, as I say now, that it will be difficult to bargain on the one hand for clarified, tougher and enforceable national standards for medicare when, on the other hand, payments to provincial governments are being reduced.
Nevertheless, in spite of the regrettable mistake of this spring, I wish the minister well in her efforts to bring in, with provincial approval, a new Canada health care act by next year. This would consolidate all existing legislation and incorporate new ways to maintain and strengthen the principles and quality of medicare. It will not be easy to do this when there are so many Conservative governments that are, at heart, actually hostile to medicare for long-standing ideological reasons.
If I have time, I should like to address another related matter. Recently, the Canadian Medical Association commenced a study on the rationalization of health care, claiming that under-funding is causing doctors to have to make life and death decisions, and that some way will have to be found to decide who will receive treatment and who will not. This is a
vicious tactic by the doctors and shows how low their leaders are prepared to stoop. It is embarrassing I am sure, to the many fine, dedicated physicians who still live and work in Canada.
The question of rationalization will not go away. It must be dealt with. Before medicare, the marketplace, tempered by the discretion of altruistic doctors, rationalized health care in this country. Medicare was intended to overcome this problem and it did. As long as there was economic growth and abundant funding, there were no great structural problems. Now that we are in the era of the shrinking economic pie, however, the principles of medicare are being tested.
The response of some, like the Canadian Medical Association, has been to argue for the reintroduction of private, user-based funding which will mean a return to rationalization by the marketplace. Those of us who favour single-source public sector funding will have to do more than just dig in against private funding mechanisms. We will have to find a way to make sure that health care is not rationalized by politics, per se, by federal provincial disputes over funding and by economic policy in general. Perhaps we will have to find a way to separate health funding from the raising of general revenue by governments, so that people can support increased health funding without giving up their opposition to government spending policies in general. Otherwise, Mr. Speaker, the pressure to reintroduce private money into our underfunded system will become unbearable, and people will finally rebel against the rationalization of health care, and thus their very lives, by the ministers of finance of the country.
This problem must be faced and solved. It must be faced and solved by pro-medicare people, or the anti-medicare people, of whom there are more than meets the eye, will eventually win the day. I invite the minister to respond to these observations.

speakeroldname: Mr. Henri Tousignant (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: MEDICAL CARE-EXTRA BILLING BY PHYSICIANS-MINISTER'S POSITION. (B) FEDERAL FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member rushing his question. He knows I only have a few minutes and that I read slowly, so that helps me. I also appreciate your indulgence, Mr. Speaker.
In reply to the hon. member's question, the position of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) with respect to extra billing is well known. It has been the goal and belief of the minister, reinforced and supported by the views expressed by Mr. Justice Hall and the majority of the members of the parliamentary task force on federal fiscal arrangements, that extra billing should be eliminated. The way to achieve this goal is through the co-operation of the provincial governments. As you know, the division of responsibilities under the Constitution does not permit the federal government to unilaterally legislate on the delivery of personal health care. Any actions taken by the federal government must not be regulatory in matters falling within provincial jurisdictions. We were able to implement national health insurance programs through provincial co-operation. Therefore, in order to
July 15, 1982

maintain these programs, it is essential that the conditions for the federal contributions be as fully acceptable as possible to provincial governments. The federal government wishes to strengthen national Medicare, not take any action which will weaken or destroy it.
At the May 26, 1982, federal-provincial conference, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) expressed her goal in her opening statement as follows: "I would hope that all of us can agree that we must take steps to eliminate extra billing." It was the minister's hope that all provincial ministers of health would be prepared to work towards the elimination of this practice. As it happened, this was not the case. They did agree, however, that control of extra billing must be addressed in order to protect accessibility-
In this regard, the Minister of National Health and Welfare was certainly successful in moving the provinces closer to the federal government's view, in that for the first time all provincial ministers are in agreement that extra billing is a problem
Adjournment Debate
which could be a threat to medicare, and its control is essential. The question of extra billing is now one that will be addressed. Controlling it will be part of program conditions aimed at ensuring that medicare is accessible. The Minister of National Health and Welfare is pleased with, and enthusiastic about, the demonstrated determination of the provincial ministers of health to approach upcoming discussions with a spirit of openness and co-operation. Proposals made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare are to be discussed at the ministerial and official level prior to the next conference of federal and provincial ministers, presently envisaged for this fall. These discussions are already under way. A significant step forward has been taken toward strengthening medicare for all Canadians. I hope this answer will satisfy the hon. member.
